speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED COURSE OP ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish at this time to make a brief statement and a suggestion about the business of the house and the business of the country. I want to suggest to all hon. members, and particularly to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the leaders of the other parties opposite, that we should consider carefully whether it might not be possible to reach agreement on a course of action to meet a serious aspect of the situation now facing this house. I would ask the leaders opposite not to give me an immediate answer but to consider what I am about to say and to let me know before the house meets on Monday whether they would be agreeable to following the course I am going to suggest.
All hon. members are, of course, aware that the interim supply voted to defray the cost of administering the affairs of this country since April 1 is virtually exhausted and that, unless additional money to carry on the administration is voted at an early date, many thousands of people in this country will be faced with inconvenience and even serious embarrassment. It seems to me that all our fellow citizens do expect this parliament to conduct the nation's business in such a fashion that party warfare, which is inseparable from our form of government, does not result in unnecessary inconvenience and hardship to the people of Canada whom we are all here to serve.
In other sessions it has been usual at this stage for the government to ask for and for the opposition to agree to the voting of one month's interim supply in order to permit the administration of the affairs of the country to be carried on while the work of the session continues. To do so now would not deprive members of the opposition of the means of continuing their opposition to the government. There are many contentious items on the order paper about which it would be possible for hon. gentlemen opposite who wish to do so to oppose the government as strongly as they feel they would be justified in doing. I would, therefore, hope sincerely that it might be possible for the parties 67509-307
opposite to accept this suggestion I am making that we should proceed on Monday by agreement to the granting of interim supply for one month in the usual way.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposiiion):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED COURSE OP ACTION
speechtext:
This statement sounds very
plausible but is in keeping with the manner in which I regret to say the Prime Minister has put forward certain other suggestions within the past few days. What should be remembered is that this house does not yet know what the plans of the government are in regard to the continuance of this session. What would ordinarily be regarded as sources extremely close to the government have been stating it is the intention of the government to adjourn within a short time. If an adjournment is to take place, it presents an entirely different situation than that with which we would ordinarily be confronted.
Before we speak of other matters, I should think that the government would be only accepting its responsibilities to the house, all of which form a part of the general responsibilities of parliament, in telling us what it is the intention of the government to do. The Prime Minister has said that it seems all our people expect us to conduct our affairs in a way that will not cause disadvantage to the people of Canada. I would point out that it has been the custom to bring down interim supply before the earlier supply had come to an end. This is now June 8, and supply came to an end on May 31. I regret to say that this is only in keeping with the manner in which much of the business of the house is done, that we should be asked to vote interim supply at a time when the supply has already expired.
Naturally we will be ready at any time to consider any proposals, but since the Prime Minister has seen fit, and that of course is his right, to make this statement in the house before it has been communicated to me as Leader of the Opposition or to the leaders of the other parties, I believe it is appropriate to reply also in the house and to say that before suggestions are made as to the way in which business should be done in regard to the details now before us, it would be most appropriate if the government would inform us as to whether it intends to continue this session without interruption until our business is completed or whether it is intended to adjourn the house. This would have a very

Business of the House definite bearing upon the voting of interim supply without any examination of the details now before us.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED COURSE OP ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish merely to say on behalf of this group that even as we have been giving all these matters serious consideration for many days, we shall continue to give serious consideration to the situation that now confronts not only this country and the house but the government. Like the Leader of the Opposition we feel that before we are asked for an answer more information should be given to us than has been indicated by the Prime Minister this morning.
So far as this issue is concerned, I would remind the Prime Minister and the government that several days before the end of May I began to ask the Minister of Finance questions regarding interim supply. I made it clear that we were conscious of the fact that interim supply was running out and that in our view the normal course was for the government to bring down interim supply before the date that the money already on hand had run out.
However, Mr. Speaker, at this point I merely wish to indicate that, as we have been doing, we will continue to give consideration to the situation.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED COURSE OP ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we will be prepared to give careful consideration to what the Prime Minister has suggested. At the moment I see no relationship whatsoever between the need to have interim supply for the period of one month and the future plans of the government with regard to adjournment or to any possible adjournment. They need the money; the bills have to be paid. We have never yet taken more than a couple of hours at any time, so far as I can remember, to vote as much as two months' supply. However, so far as we are concerned we shall be prepared to join with others in giving careful consideration to the Prime Minister's suggestion and on Monday we shall let him know exactly what we decide.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED COURSE OP ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am sorry that it is not possible at the present time to announce, or even to make, any plans for the future course of this session. This matter of interim supply is one of immediate urgency and I would hope that it would be considered in that aspect and as a routine matter that could be dealt with in the usual way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED COURSE OP ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish in any way to engage in a debate on this subject but I would point out that it is now June


8, and if there is any foundation whatsoever for the statements that are appearing in the press that it is the intention of the government to adjourn before the end of June, that is now known to the government. To say that the government is not in a position to inform the house as to what its intentions are is straining the credulity of the members of this house rather severely.
The point I wish to make is this. We certainly have no desire to see anyone suffer as the result of the failure of the government to conduct its business in the ordinary way. Nevertheless, the government has seen fit not to follow the ordinary course by delaying the introduction of supply until some time after it would ordinarily come before the house. The extent to which it would be appropriate for us to facilitate the discussion of this subject depends on many things- and certainly we are as anxious as the government is that there should be no inconvenience to any Canadian because of proceedings here-but the fact is that we should know before we give an answer of that kind whether it is the intention of the government to adjourn the house and in that way postpone all consideration of the estimates where it will be possible for us actually to examine the business of the people of Canada. Obviously, that creates an entirely different situation. If we are to proceed without interruption to deal with the estimates such as those of national defence and other departments which are large spending departments and of extreme importance, or if on the other hand there is to be a deferment until a date when the major part of the expenditure will already have taken place, or have been committed for the remainder of the year, I do think the Prime Minister should be in a position to tell us the intention of the government with regard to adjournment. I cannot believe there are any uncertainties at the present time which would make it impossible for the Prime Minister to give that information to the house which at this stage of the session he should be able to give.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

Now, what has taken place is of such a character that we shall have to reconsider whether or not it would be possible to make that suggestion to the house with any hope that it would meet with the approval of the house.

The house resumed, from Thursday, June 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Drew:
In view of the unprecedented action of Mr. Speaker in (a) improperly reversing his own decision without notice and without giving any opportunity for discussion; (b) repeatedly refusing to allow members to address the house on occasions when the rules provide that they have the right to be heard; (c) subordinating the rights of the house to the will of the government, this house resolves that it no longer has any confidence in its presiding officer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the house would generally agree that my paraphrasing of the observations of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) clearly establishes his high regard for the Speaker as a man and particularly, because it is more relevant in this context, his great confidence in the particular role which he has in this house, and that that confidence prevailed, as far as the hon. member is concerned, up until a point somewhere between ten o'clock on Thursday, May 31, and the 1st of June. That was not, however, the view of the hon. gentleman who leads the party which my hon. friend supports, for the leader of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation said at page 4650 of the current Hansard that what he had heard in the pipe line debate was evidence of what he called partisan rulings and the Leader of the Opposition in his carefully and moderately uttered statement observed that there had been rumblings about the quality of the Speaker long before the pipe line debate began; sometime, presumably, during the course of the recent winter. It is clear, however, that as far as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was concerned his alleged confidence was shaken only at the time I have indicated. He has said that the Speaker did not act independently.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have always understood that argument by assertion is not in fact argument at all. For one hon. member to say that the Speaker did not act independently is not in any way to establish with any justification that he did not in fact act independently. I can understand my hon. friend saying that perhaps of others with whom he did not enjoy the same measure of acknowledged and avowed intimacy and the cordial relationship which he 67509-307i
House of Commons
had with the Speaker, the man who was his friend up until that period of May 31.

speechtext:
June 1. This is what Mr. Speaker said at page 4539 of the current Hansard about whether or not he had acted independently:
I want to tell hon. members that I know what my responsibilities are and that I am fully conscious of every step that I am taking.
Then he went on:
I am prepared to take responsibility before this house and the country for what I do.
The Speaker says he has acted independently and if my hon. friend really means to establish, as I know he does, his regard for the Speaker, this great friendship which has prevailed up until the very last moment, then I do not know what canon of fairness would suggest to my hon. friend to make an assertion that the Speaker did not in this matter act independently. Are we to have guilt by association, accusation by insinuation, and slander by smear, particularly of one's friend, the man who holds the highest office in the gift of this house?
I noticed that when the Prime Minister was speaking the other day the leader of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation applauded the Prime Minister's observation that all or most of us in this house have regard for His Honour the Speaker. The leader of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation applauded that remark. I am at a loss to understand that kind of gesture. If the Speaker of this house was deserving of the implications of this motion, supported by the hon. members I have mentioned, I do not know how they can say that they have regard for the Speaker.
Mr. Gladstone once said when he was bitterly attacked that he did not want the friendship and the fulsome praise of his opponents who had branded his remarks as not capable of measuring up to the truth. I will not carry on the logical implication that flows from this reference to Mr. Gladstone, but it surely on reflection must apply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who I believe is sincere when he says that he has friendship for the Speaker. Not in any part of his speech, which I read three times since it was delivered last night; not in any place has there been any kind of evidence by which one friend would judge another friend to be guilty of impropriety.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has presented us with a motion. He did not go as far as the hon. member for Winnipeg

House of Commons
North Centre, but I think his motion deserves to be read at this time. It reads:
In view of the unprecedented action of Mr. Speaker in (a) improperly reversing his own decision without notice and without giving any opportunity for discussion; (b) repeatedly refusing to allow members to address the house on occasions when the rules provide that they have the right to be heard; (c) subordinating the rights of the house to the will of the government, this house resolves that it no longer has any confidence in its presiding officer.
Mr. Speaker, the very wording of that resolution without any supporting speeches is justification for not accepting the motion at all. Assuming that the Speaker did not give notice and did reverse his own decision, does that constitute a basis for a motion of censure? Supposing the Speaker did refuse to allow members on occasion to speak on points on which they felt they had a right to be heard, is that justification for a motion of censure?
I do not agree that the Speaker reversed himself, but I am prepared to argue that even if he had, at best he could be accused or charged with an error of judgment, with misinterpretation of the rules. But in the absence of intention to be malicious and mischievous he certainly does not under our practice in this house or in the British House of Commons warrant the accusation and implication involved in a motion of censure. He clearly did not reverse himself. At page 4531 of Hansard of May 31 the Speaker is reported as having said:
It would seem to me, however, that in a matter of this kind the thing to do, after having placed ourselves in a position where we can deal with the matter, especially since I am concerned, is to postpone the consideration of that motion.
I am trying to save time, and I quote now from page 4532, where the Speaker continues as follows:
-I am not going to object; I am just going to let them go right ahead, but at one stage of the proceedings I want to say that I will have to be heard.
Then at page 4539 the Speaker made his ruling. He said:
I am prepared to take the responsibility before this house and the country for what I do . . . Today we meet; I make a ruling.
There is nothing to suggest, as this motion suggests, that the Speaker had in any way reversed a decision which he had taken the night before.

I shall come to that at the end of my statement. I have read the speech of the Leader of the Opposition and I think it was, having in mind the context of the preceding days, an admirable example of restraint, but let any member of this house read every word of that speech and he will not find one accusation against the Speaker that would justify our resorting to what Mr. Herbert Morrison has called the rarely used technique of challenging in a fundamental position the authority of the Speaker.
There was never any suggestion by the Leader of the Opposition that the Speaker had not acted independently; he had reversed his decision; he had refused to listen to members who raised points of order; and on that account-and on that account alone -he deserved to be censured by this house. I do not believe that anyone can argue that it is the obligation of the Speaker to permit, or that he is allowed to permit, a debate on a point of order. When the Speaker does permit members to speak to a point of order, they appear before him as amici curiae, friends of the court, but not debating a proposition, with no right to debate the question. If that is the case, how can the Leader of the Opposition suggest that the Speaker at any time refused to permit hon. members to speak?
Even if he had refused them to speak, are we bound only by the letter of our rules? Do we not, in the conduct of any democratic proceeding, in this country or in the western world, recognize that the presiding officer has the right at any time, where the rules do not precisely cover a situation, to use his discretion as to what in the best interests of all concerned is the proper, orderly way in which to proceed? Surely the Speaker must be allowed that kind of discretion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
My hon. friend makes that point, and I am prepared to say this. Even if what he says were true, I would say that this is not a justification for taking the man who holds the highest office in the house of this free parliament and subjecting him to all that flows from a vote of censure. That is what I say. I find that perhaps no one has stated the situation more effectively than has the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). I want to remind the house of some of the observations he made before I come to a point that I regard as being extremely important. He had been referring to the background of the controversy-and I use that phrase in order to be as objective as possible in my presentation-one that undoubtedly taxed the patience and ingenuity of the Speaker. Here is what the hon. member for Acadia said as reported at page 4653 of Hansard:
In my opinion the Speaker has always been lenient in listening to advice on points of order and unfortunately instead of appreciating that the opposition has abused it.
Those are the words of the hon. member for Acadia, not mine. Then he goes on to quote the first part of the resolution as follows:
In view of the unprecedented action of Mr. Speaker in (a) improperly reversing his own decision without notice and without giving any opportunity for discussion;-
Then the hon. member for Acadia continues as follows:
We in this group are of the opinion that on Thursday the Speaker did make a mistake in rendering his decision regarding the point brought up by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron). If that situation had been left as it was then it would have created a precedent that would have brought chaos into this house in the future. It would have meant that at any time any hon. member in this house disliked legislation the government sought to introduce and wanted to obstruct it, all he would have to do would be to get a friend of his to write a letter to the press and then bring it up, as did the hon. member for Nanaimo, and we would have obstruction without end because every time a letter is written to the press it could then be raised as a point of privilege in this house, and there would be no end to those points of privilege.
House of Commons
Mr. Speaker, is not that the true assessment of this whole situation? The Speaker was confronted with an unusual situation. There is nothing in our rules which says that, in regard to that kind of a situation, the Speaker cannot use his own discretion as to the best conceivable way of bringing about order. If he had not taken the step that he took, we would not have had whatever degree of order later followed and continued. This statement of the hon. member for Acadia perhaps represented only his own assessment of the situation. He may possibly not have known that he was expressing a view that is not only within our tradition but is part and parcel of the very rules which we operate here and under which parliament operates in the United Kingdom. I was not aware of that fact until early this morning when I took oil my library shelf a book written by Herbert Morrison, entitled "Government and Parliament". At page 200 I find this reference which I will read. He was speaking about discussion, private members' rights, closure and so on; the actual title of the chapter is "The Closure". At page 202 he said this:
For example, although there had been talk about the need to expedite business by curtailing private members' rights, it was only in the panic which followed the successful Irish obstruction in the 1880's that the house parted with its long preserved liberties. One of the most far-reaching of these reforms was the closure (that is to say, the motion 'That the question be now put'). It was first used by Mr. Speaker Brand, on 2 February 1881, who, in the course of a long debate and considerable obstruction, decided to put the question without further debate. He made a dignified statement saying that he considered that a crisis had arisen in parliamentary procedure and that the tedious discussions were against the general sense of the house.
That is the important thing-"against the general sense of the house". The quotation contains:
He ended by saying that further measure for ensuring orderly debate must be left to the judgment of the house, meaning either that the government must take responsibility by bringing forward appropriate orders or that the house itself must find ways and means of solving the problem.
That is the commentary of Mr. Morrison who spoke for his party on procedural matters in the House of Commons during the years from 1945 to 1951 and who wrote this admirable book which includes many references to procedural questions. After much difficulty and with the help of the librarian I recovered the parliamentary debates that were in the hands of one hon. member opposite, and I refer the house to what Mr. Speaker Brand said in 1881 as recorded in Hansard for that year. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knows, Mr. Speaker Brand was one of the great Speakers of all time, whose decisions are constantly

House of Commons
referred to. He has been referred to by Mr. Churchill as the kind of man who furnishes the standards by which he who presides over our proceedings shall be judged. Mr. Gladstone in 1882 moved closure because of the circumstances that attended the debate on the Irish bill in 1880 and 1881.

I will come to that. But Mr. Speaker Brand, confronted with a situation for which there was no provision in the rules for the remedial action which he might take, had to give consideration as to whether or not the sense of the house-the sense of the situation, the desirabilities in the matter which every man under our system, even though it may not be written, clearly understands is proper on occasion to have applied. What did he say? Here is what Mr. Speaker said on that occasion. It is the kind of thing that the hon. member for Acadia envisaged in his own excellent observation. Mr. Speaker Brand,- and this is before the closure-with no justification by anything embodied in the rules of parliament, was acting as I say in appreciation of what he felt was the sense of the situation, just as our Mr. Speaker acted, I submit, last Friday in accordance with what he thought, in his best judgment, honestly conceived, was the sense of the situation. I will at once endow hon. members opposite with the right to take issue with this statement of mine, but in the absence of being able to establish that the Speaker did not act honourably, this motion has not the slightest justification for presentation in this house. Here is what Mr. Speaker Brand said:
A crisis has thus arisen which demands the prompt interposition of the Chair, and of the House. The usual rules have proved powerless to ensure orderly and effective debate. An important measure, recommended in Her Majesty's Speech nearly a month since, and declared to be urgent, in the interests of the State, by a decisive majority, is being arrested by the action of an inconsiderable minority, the Members of which have resorted to those modes of ''Obstruction", which have been recognized by the House as a Parliamentary offence.
The dignity, the credit, and the authority of this House are seriously threatened, and it is necessary that they should be vindicated. Under the operation of the accustomed rules and methods of procedure, the Legislative Powers of the House are paralysed. A new and exceptional course is imperatively demanded: and I am satisfied that I shall best carry out the will of the House, and may rely upon its support, if I decline to call upon any more Members to speak, and at once proceed to put the Question from the Chair. I feel assured that the House will be prepared to exercise all its powers in giving effect to these proceedings.
... I am satisfied that I shall best carry out the will of the House, and may rely upon its support,

if I decline to call upon any more members to speak, and at once proceed to put the Question from the Chair.
If that is not the most classical justification for the decision taken by Mr. Speaker, the friend of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), his most cherished friend, the man who knows more about the rules of this house, it is said, than anyone else, then I do not understand the implications of the language of Mr. Speaker Brand.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: You have not yet told us how long that debate had gone on.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition will remember the circumstances under which he himself, in 1947, urged in the Ontario legislature that the question be now put. That was an unusual procedure. The hon. gentleman, when he comes to speak, will tell me whether or not I am correct in saying that that procedure is not embodied in the rules of the Ontario legislature. There was some question about the authority taken by the Speaker, that is whether or not he was justified in the circumstances. I am sure that the Speaker of the day in the Ontario legislature, as the hon. gentleman, could make a strong argument for the course he had taken. In any event, those who opposed that course would not have had the justification of challenging the authority of the Speaker or saying that he had acted improperly or dishonourably.
There are three alternatives before us in this matter. We have said that none of us like this situation. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that when he spoke. We have heard the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) say that this was an unfortunate matter to have to deal with. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) said he did not like it either. The leader of this government, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), proposed that the motion be withdrawn but the hon. member for Prince Albert said, speaking in the name of his party, he would not accept the Prime Minister's suggestion. What are the alternatives? The suggestion that an unnecessary election should be imposed at this time on the people would settle nothing. It would not settle this issue. This issue, under our traditions and under our rules, can only be settled in one place and by one group of men and that is by those of us who at this time constitute the House of Commons.
Mr. Herbert Morrison recognized that was the case, for at page 204 of his book on "Government and Parliament" he writes:
Motions can be put on the order paper criticising or even censuring the conduct of the Speaker or

his deputy (the chairman of ways and means) or the deputy chairman of ways and means. These may then be debated and may even be voted upon. Such occasions, fortunately, are very rare.
But they do happen, and on the occasions when they do happen the way that they are resolved is by the house concerned taking a decision as was taken in 1881 and in 1882 in Her Majesty's parliament in the United Kingdom. So, if we cannot have this problem resolved by the acceptance of one of these two alternatives I have mentioned, then what is shameful in this house being called upon to make a decision? Who is more competent than the members of this house who have watched Mr. Speaker operate over the past three and a half years? Are they not the ones who can best decide whether or not he deserves our continued confidence? Speaking as one member in this house, I have every confidence in Mr. Speaker. For three years he has discharged his responsibilities with honour, impartiality and maturity. I may say that I thought sometimes he permitted too much general discussion on points of order which in the final analysis he alone had to decide. But of course that is not a valid argument against him. It is in his favour as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said last night.
I see no justification but one for this motion that is before us at this time. It is one that I wish the Leader of the Opposition, who is an officer of this house and who holds a very responsible post just as the Prime Minister does, will see fit at some time to dispose of in a manner which will be in accord with our traditions and in accord with the dignity and the proper functioning of our deliberations. But that is not for me to say. I simply say, as one member of this house, that I have confidence in Mr. Speaker and I continue to have that confidence. I see no justification in this attempted censuring of a man who, admittedly on all sides, has acted so creditably throughout his speakership.
The Leader of the Opposition reminded us of what Mr. Speaker said when on November 12, 1953, he spoke to this house on assuming his high office. Mr. Speaker said, amongst other things:
I shall, I assure you, strive to deserve your effective support, and endeavour at all times to prove myself worthy of your trust.
Is there any hon. member in this house who will divorce himself from the incidents of the past weeks or who will confront those incidents objectively who can authoritatively assert that the Speaker has not sincerely carried out his trust? What evidence exists anywhere for any suggestion to the contrary? If there is no evidence, mere innuendo, mere insinuation, is not worthy of any hon.
House of Commons
member in this house. He is a man whose office is a symbol as well as the prop of the existence of this institution.
My final words are these. I am not misled by this resolution. It is not the Speaker who is the real target of this attack, it is the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: It is the government that is sought after by this motion by the hon. member who now says, "Hear, hear". It is not Mr. Speaker, it is the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: We are after the government for what you did to our Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: In their eager desire to try to force on the people an unnecessary election which will not resolve this question, some of my hon. friends opposite care not, Samsonlike, if they pull down the Speaker's chair and the pillars of parliament along with it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, even as the minister asked me a question the other night at the end of my speech, I am sure he will permit me to ask him one before he concludes. Is he not aware that it is precisely because of my regard for Mr. Speaker that what the government has done to him is so tragic?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am glad the hon. gentleman has asked me this question because it clearly confirms what I said at the end of my speech, that it is not the Speaker whom hon. gentlemen opposite are challenging in this house, it is the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: For what the government has done to Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: No matter what the government has done it is no justification for pulling down the reputation and the authority of the Speaker of the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has just concluded an address in which I found it rather difficult to perceive any consistent argument. In concluding this speech he used a simile or metaphor in which he accused the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and, by inference, all the opposition of acting in a manner similar to that of Samson when he destroyed the temple by pulling down the pillars. If that simile has any application may I remind the minister and hon. members opposite that Samson's actions were brought about inevitably-the tragedy of Samson's actions was brought about-because he had been betrayed. He had been delivered into the hands of the iniquitous by Delilah.

House of Commons
Perhaps, there is some applicable simile here. The government has betrayed not only the Speaker but the House of Commons and parliament, and it was the government's betrayal of its responsibility and of its trust as equal custodians, with the others of us who sit here, of the rights of parliament, that had the result, if it has that result, of pulling the pillars and bringing the edifice crashing down. The responsibility rests with the government. But, sir, that is about the only part of the minister's speech that had any practical application to the situation now before us.
The minister tried to pretend-I will not say "tried to pretend"-the minister said that he somehow or other found this motion of censure almost repulsive, that there was something horrifying in the fact that it should have been moved. I can assure him and assure you, sir, if the assurance is necessary-I think indeed the statement has already been accepted by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Finance- that the motion was not moved lightly, nor was it moved except after there had been some opportunity for mature consideration. It is true that we base the necessity for the motion on the fact that the government has produced the situation which gives rise to the motion. But let me remind the ministers, particularly the Minister of National Health and Welfare, that all during the time of this steady deterioration of the relationship between the house and the Speaker, all during the course of this debate when consistently and time and time again precedent piled upon precedent, what we sincerely regarded-and I submit shall be able to demonstrate-as incorrect rulings were given and incorrect actions were taken;-when those actions were protested to the Speaker, when we sought to bring the relationship back on an even keel and to remind the Speaker and the government of the rights and privileges which it is the duty of the Speaker to protect-nevertheless, instead of our course succeeding in restoring the balance, it resulted on at least two occasions, and I believe it may have been on three, in the Speaker virtually challenging us to move a motion of censure. The Minister of Finance shakes his head.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: He will find absolute proof of what I say in Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I did not shake my head in either agreement or disagreement.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I take it, then, that the minister accepts as a fact what I have said. It is a fact, as can be seen by consulting the record.

The Minister of Finance made a speech yesterday in which he, in effect, held out the olive branch and invited us to forget everything. He invited us, as it were, to say to ourselves, "Well, we moved this motion of censure in a fit of very strong emotion. Perhaps tve were justified in moving it under the turmoil of the emotion then prevailing, but now that it is all over perhaps the best thing to do would be to withdraw the motion and to forget the situation which gave rise to it".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I never said that.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance says that he did not say that. I took it from his speech. I hope I am not being unfair. If he says that was not his intention I will accept it, but I do say-I am sure I am accurate here- that he hoped that when this was all over the old relationships would be resumed and that parliament would be able to carry on regardless of what had happened. Sir, I have some doubts as to whether that is possible. Certainly, all of us must try to carry on in the proper relationships that should prevail between government and opposition and to that end I certainly-and I am quite sure my colleagues will subscribe to this

shall try to do that. But I assure you, sir, that it is going to be extremely difficult because it is not going to be easy, indeed, it may not be possible, ever to wipe out the recollection of what was done to parliament by the government, and I do not see how it is going to be possible ever to restore the relationships to what they were before and to what it might be desirable to have them in this parliament, because the government that did that to parliament is the same government we still see here and will see here until this house is dissolved.
As I followed the Minister of Finance yesterday and as I read his speech in Hansard, I tried to understand the argument that he put forward to us, and I must confess that I have not been able to get any very clear interpretation of his argument. That may well be my fault. I know the minister is capable of putting forward a clear argument and does so on most occasions, even though we do not necessarily agree with him. On this occasion I find it difficult to draw out of his speech a clear argument as to what gave rise to the situation and what should be done about it. About the main argument I draw from his speech of yesterday is that under our system, with Speakers appointed and changed every parliament, it is difficult, if not impossible, to get an impartial Speaker and difficult, if not impossible, to achieve a situation where the Speaker's ruling would be viewed impartially.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am afraid I did shake my head in negation of that one.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The minister says he did not say that, but I refer him to two passages on page 4810 of Hansard, which certainly come very close to saying that. In the first he said:
Let me ask hon. members opposite, is there any solution to dissatisfaction with a ruling of the Speaker except to put it to a vote of the house and to have a vote in which in all likelihood there would be a party division? So long as we have appeals that is bound to be the outcome in most eases.
Then he went on to say later on:
When hon. members opposite in this particular matter express regret that we shall not be able to come to a conclusion except on what they think is a partisan vote, let me point out that since I came to parliament, and long before that, appeals with respect to the Speaker's rulings were decided in that particular way. Now, it surely is a matter for consideration that if that is the case, one wonders whether any useful purpose is served except to continue to remind the Speaker that there are members in the house who disagree with him, and nothing much beyond that.
It did seem to me-and I may be wrong but this is my interpretation of the main import of the minister's argument-he may say this is not what he intended, and, if so, I accept it-that under our system it is difficult if not impossible, to get impartial rulings and to get rulings accepted as impartial and regarded as impartial by members on different sides of the house. I do not accept that view but I take it to be the minister's.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: That is not my view.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Very well; the minister says that is not his view. I wish he would interpret his argument for us on some other occasion. But I do say that what he actually said, whether or not my view of his argument be correct, emphasizes the necessity of the government's being scrupulously careful in its relationship to the Speaker, being scrupulous not to place any burden on the Speaker which would make him less able to be impartial, not to enter into any relationship with him or to embark upon any course of conduct in the house that will make it difficult for the Speaker to be impartial. I submit, sir, that the government's course in the conduct of this debate particularly has not measured up to that standard of scrupulous conduct that is necessary.
The Minister of Finance did not deny yesterday having a meeting with the Speaker after ten o'clock on Thursday night. He denied the passing of a certain note but he did not deny-and I submit that no one over there can deny-that they made every effort and in fact succeeded in the course of this debate in influencing the Speaker in the judgments and decisions and rulings he was about to give.
House of Commons

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, to deny at this point that I at any time influenced the Speaker in any manner whatsoever in the course of the debate.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Well, sir, I shall come in a few moments to some representations concerning what was seen in this house both by members of the press gallery and by hon. members, and I shall state what I myself saw in connection with a certain incident in the course of the debate. Before I get to that, however, let me deal with another matter the Minister of Finance dealt with in the course of his remarks. He said we should not blame the Speaker because the government imposed closure. I quite agree and I take it that the implication of the minister's remarks is that he felt it was possible that we in a spell of poor judgment, shall I say, were in fact without realizing it taking out our anger and our concern by a motion of censure on the Speaker, our anger having been aroused by the fact that the government introduced closure. Let me assure him, sir, that is not the case, as I have already pointed out.
Let me then return to the minister's argument. I agree with him that one should not blame the Speaker because the government imposed closure. No; but I do say that when closure is applied then the Speaker must be more careful than ever, more concerned than ever, to preserve the rights of the minority, because closure is of course the most violent, the most tremendous imposition that can be made on the ordinary rights of the minority. It is a method which is provided under the rules of the house although its application in this case, I still maintain, was not in accordance with the rules of the house; nevertheless, it is a method provided for. However, when it is invoked then the Speaker, the protector and the ultimate custodian of the rights of the house, must be more careful than ever to see that those rules which protect the minority even under closure are scrupulously observed; and unfortunately, sir, instead of that happening we saw the contrary.
After the application of closure by the government we saw a steady deterioration in the regard of the Chair for the rights of the minority which had become so much more important by virtue of the application of closure, and we saw-and the minister must accept what I say-what we believe to be a deterioration in the regard and the care of the Speaker for those rights under the pressure of the government.
I regret to say, as a matter of fact, that in the course of this debate the Chair as a

House of Commons
whole came into disrepute. We have one Speaker, it is true, but the Chair is shared by the three presiding officers-the Speaker, Deputy Speaker and deputy chairman-who normally rotate, and the pressure was such that in my view the Chair as a whole was brought into disrepute by the pressure applied by the government in the course of this debate, pressure applied as a result of its desire not only to invoke closure but to make closure as restrictive, and improperly restrictive, as it could possibly do.
There are three branches of the motion of censure before the house and I should like to deal with the central or middle branch first; that is, with the portion dealing with the action of Mr. Speaker in repeatedly refusing to allow members to address the house on occasions when the rules provide they have the right to be heard.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) said there is not a shred of evidence of the improper conduct which is alleged against the Speaker or against the Chair, but just previous to that he had dismissed one of the very substantial pieces of evidence that we had brought; that is, the disregarding of the rights of members with respect to points of order and questions of privilege. The minister dismissed that as irrelevant, saying that the Speaker may have refused to see an occasional member but after all the Speaker is the final judge. But disregard of the rules is what we are complaining about, and how can the minister say, in view of the actions of the Chair in refusing to hear points of order and questions of privilege, that we have not brought evidence to substantiate the motion?
I would remind you, sir, that under standing order 17, and by virtue of the provisions of citation 110 of Beauchesne's third edition, it is clearly provided that a question of privilege or a point of order must be taken into consideration whenever it is raised. That is what is stated: "must be taken into consideration,"-and yet what did we see? Repeatedly we saw members disregarded on points of order and questions of privilege. As a matter of fact, it went so far that on one occasion the chairman stated that he deliberately disregarded members who rose, deliberately ignored them. You will find that at page 4560 of Hansard, where the deputy chairman admitted that he had deliberately ignored members who rose on points of order and questions of privilege. Why did he deliberately ignore them? He ignored them in order that he might put the question desired by the government before its propriety could be brought into question. Now, if that is not serving the purposes of the government then

I do not know the plain meaning of ordinary words; but that was done, notwithstanding the rule which made it an improper act on the part of the chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Order. The hon. member at one point mentioned the chairman and at another point mentioned the deputy chairman. My recollection is that I made no such statement. I wonder if the hon. member would clarify that for me?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Yes. It is found at page 4560 of Hansard and it is made clear it was the deputy chairman who was concerned at that moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I suppose the hon. gentleman would not be willing to permit a question?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Yes, if it is short.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: It is very short.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: We would be glad to have a speech from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman contend the standing order he referred to gives any member a right to rise on a point of order when the chairman himself has the floor?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, citation 110 reads:
Points of order are questions raised with the view of calling attention to any departure from the standing orders or the customary modes of proceeding in debate or in the conduct of legislative business, and may be raised at any time by any member, whether he has previously spoken or not.
Now, sir, in order that I might deal with the question raised by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) let me say that on the occasion to which I refer- and I know of other occasions-members rose before the chairman rose; practically simultaneously perhaps, but in my recollection, before the chairman rose. What is material, however, is what the chairman said. I am reading from page 4560:
I was not unaware that one or more members were on their feet desiring to raise either points of order or questions of privilege, which I do not know. I did not hear them; I did not see them, let there be no doubt about that. I knew they were there but I did not officially recognize them. I consider that I was right in my action.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: You deliberately ignored them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I did not officially
recognize them. I consider-

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Put it the straight way and say that you deliberately ignored them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: If the hon. member prefers that expression I will not argue about it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: If the Chairman is accepting that as a statement of his position, that he deliberately ignored members, how can we continue on that basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
permit one more question?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I hope to be finished before the end of my 40 minutes, and perhaps the minister will therefore defer his remarks.
Let me now go back to the first branch of the motion of censure, that the Speaker improperly reversed his own decision without notice and without giving any opportunity for discussion.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest that these things can be raised during a division?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I heard the hon. gentleman's question, but these points of order and questions of privilege were not raised in the course of a division. We did try to raise some of them but many of them were not raised in the course of a division.
The chairman and Mr. Speaker on many occasions simply refused to recognize us or to hear members who were raising points of order or questions of privilege which it was their right to do. That refusal on the part of the Chair was in direct contravention of the rules and precedents of this house.
I said I was coming back to the first part of our motion of censure, that the Speaker improperly reversed his own decision without notice and without giving any opportunity for discussion. Standing order 34-this is the sort of evidence which the Minister of National Health and Welfare asked for-reads as follows:
Any member addressing the house, it called to order either by Mr. Speaker or on a point raised by another member, shall sit down while the point is being stated, after which he may explain.
On Friday morning, June 1, the Leader of the Opposition had the floor by virtue of standing order 7 and citation 216. The Speaker raised a point of order, which it was his right to do, but the effect of that point of order was to interrupt the speech of the Leader of the Opposition. While perhaps we should not, because we are members of the opposition, be overly assertive in stating the rights of the Leader of the Opposition, it is a fact which I think is recognized in their hearts by members and ministers opposite that the Leader of the Opposition occupies a peculiar place in the house because, as has been pointed out, he is an officer of this house. He occupies a position of peculiar priority with respect to his right to be heard. The Leader of the Opposition was interrupted by the Speaker, who raised a point of order, and the Leader of the Opposition indicated most clearly, as is shown by Hansard of June 1, his desire to speak to the point of order and also his desire to continue his speech once the point of 67509-308i
House of Commons
order had been settled. Yet notwithstanding the position just referred to, the Speaker refused to hear the Leader of the Opposition or anybody else on that point of order, in contravention of standing order 34 (1) which says that the hon. member shall sit down while the point is being stated, after which he may explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: The Speaker had made a ruling.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Which he had no right to make at that point.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: That standing order gives a right to the member concerned to speak to the point of order before the ruling.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: The Speaker had made a ruling which the hon. member knows was not open to review and was not debatable.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
That is my point, that the
Speaker made his ruling at that time improperly and in contravention of the rules of the house because the rules of the house say that when a point of order is raised the member who has the floor shall have the right to explain, in other words to speak to the point of order. He was denied that right and the Speaker, again seeking to advance the course of the government and under the influence of the terrific and terrible pressure which the government was exerting on him, improperly disregarded the rules of the house and reversed himself without giving an opportunity to anyone to discuss the point of order which he had raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to ask just one question. The argument which he is advancing is somewhat new. Does the hon. member contend that, under standing order 34, when an hon. member, not the Speaker, is speaking and a point of order is raised, Mr. Speaker is obliged, after the point of order has been stated by the one seeking to make it, to hear then the member who has the floor? In other words, is it the contention of my hon. friend that this does not permit Mr. Speaker to do either one of two things, to say that the point of order is not well taken or that the point of order is well taken, without hearing any further argument?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I think the rule speaks for
itself; it states that if a member is interrupted by a point of order, he shall sit down while the point is being stated, after which he may explain. Perhaps I should read the whole thing:
Any member addressing the house, if called to order either by Mr. Speaker or on a point raised by another member, shall sit down while the point is being stated, after which he may explain.

House of Commons
What could be clearer, whether the point is raised by Mr. Speaker or an hon. member?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Why do you not go on and read the rest?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I have read it already.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: No, "Mr. Speaker may permit debate." He may do it, he does not have to do it.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker)-I am not going to spend too much time on this point-is disregarding completely the first part of the standing order which says, "after which he may explain." Nothing could be clearer than that, that at least the member who is interrupted by the point of order may speak to the point of order if he wishes to do so. Mr. Speaker may then permit other debate subsequently, but he does not have to; but the rule says that at least the member who is interrupted may speak to it. I cannot see any other meaning that could be given to it. If my hon. friend disagrees with me, and as my time is running on, I would ask him to state his contrary arguments on a later occasion.
Dealing still with the first portion of our motion for censure, Mr. Speaker in an absolutely unheard of course of action then put a proposition to the house of his own motion. He tried to avoid having it described as a motion because Mr. Speaker realized he should not make a motion. He did in fact let his tongue slip in view of the tremendous pressure he was under and when it was actually being put he said, "Those in favour of this motion." That was corrected next day on a question of privilege.
But the rules of debate have come down to us from antiquity and they establish-I should not think that this would require any argument-that there can be nothing before the house for decision by way of a vote unless it is put in the form of a motion. How can you get a question before the house for decision except by way of a motion? The fact that the Speaker did not call it a motion but rather called it a proposition does not alter its basic nature. Mr. Speaker was not only improper in raising the matter himself but he put it forward at an improper time and in an improper manner because standing order 43 says:
All motions shall be In writing, and seconded, before being debated or put from the chair.
The motion of the Speaker did not even have a seconder, nor was it in writing. Furthermore, standing orders 41 and 42 provide that such a motion must have 48 hours' notice unless unanimous consent is obtained to put it forthwith without notice. In addition,

citation 136 of Beauchesne's third edition makes it clear, and I shall repeat it, that:
All motions referring to the business of the house should be introduced by the leader of the house.
This extraordinary proposition certainly related to the business of the house. It suggested that we wipe a whole day from our records. Here then we had the extraordinary, unprecedented and tragic situation that the Speaker rushed to the rescue of the government under pressure of such a nature that he substituted himself for the government leader in the house in advancing government business through the house.
Now, sir, I come to the third subparagraph of our motion of censure, which of course is the most important. The Speaker is accused of subordinating the rights of the house to the will of the government. I think it would be equally correct to say that the Speaker is subject to censure for having permitted the rights of the house to be subordinated to the will of the government, because that is what happened. The government imposed its will, and Mr. Speaker, no more than the others who from time to time occupied the chair in the course of this debate, was humanly not able to stand up to the pressure imposed upon him. I find it difficult to criticize him for that. I find it difficult to believe that there would be any ordinary human being, subject to the ordinary human emotions and temptations and frailties, who could withstand the pressure that this government put on this Speaker under the circumstances. But, sir, the fact that the happening may be pitiful or tragic, whichever way you like to look at it, cannot blind us to the fact that it happened, and we must record our disapproval of the happening and our censure of what happened.
But the main responsibility still rests with the government, and of course this situation arose because of the government's determination to ram this bill through and to ram this closure through and to use the most improper, violent and vicious form of closure. We have heard some discussion of closure before, but I think it is necessary to refer to it briefly again. I think it is desirable that the record should be cleared up and that the misinterpretations and distortions placed by the government on closure in the British house should be removed. We have heard ad nauseam about the number of times that closure is used in the British house and the suggestion made that it is a normal thing over there and that it is the same sort of closure as is used here, and therefore we are absurd when we protest about the use of closure four times in one session; but the British closure is entirely different.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I said that when I spoke.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
You are about the only one who did, and you said it very sotto voce. The British closure is entirely different. The British closure is what we know as the previous question, and even that takes a slightly different form from our previous question. It is true that the previous question is used over there on frequent occasions. It is true, as the Minister of Finance said, that it may be invoked in the middle of the afternoon by any member of the house, but, sir, there are these two safeguards: first, that it shall not be put if the Speaker thinks it is an undue curtailment of debate and, second, it requires the support of 100 in the house even then before it will be put.
But there is this third and most important difference which explains so clearly why it is used over there so frequently as a matter of course. The previous question is available to private members as a means of bringing about a vote on their own proposals then before the house. Here we do not have that course available. Here, if the government finds a private member's proposal embarrassing, then they can talk it out, and they do. Over there, in order to avoid that happening and in order to enable a private member to bring to a vote a proposal he puts forward, he has the device of getting one of his friends to move the previous question. Then, if the Speaker thinks that there has been adequate discussion, he puts it, because he thinks it is desirable to have a decision of the house on the matter. So the previous question applies to private legislation and private members' proposals in a way that simply does not prevail here and it is a device which helps private members get a decision on the propositions they put before the house.
That is the reason why closure is used 121 times a year, or whatever it may be, in England. To suggest that the situations are comparable is to distort the facts and to misrepresent them to the house and the country.

House of Covimons
rules. The rules applying since then provide for limitation of debate to a far greater extent than they did just a year ago. We accepted them, after negotiation and compromise. We were not happy about them, but it was better than what we would have had forced on us if we had not. We accepted a limitation on the throne speech debate and a limitation on the budget debate and a limitation to six motions for going into supply. Yet the government is trying to say that the opposition refuses to accept any limitation on debate.
Now we come to the closure rule as it was applied by this government on this occasion. This, as I have said, is what started the deterioration in the relations between the house and the Chair. The invocation of the closure rule requires the most vigorous insistence by Mr. Speaker on the scrupulous adherence to the rules which protect the minority. Instead of that, we saw a steady whittling away under government pressure, of even those ordinary rules which protect the minority.
Now I come back to the question of the pressure brought by the government on the Chair, and the evidence of it. We saw, sitting here, what my hon. friend the member for London (Mr. Mitchell) referred to as that other pipe line, the pipe line between the house leader and the Chair. I well recall, sir, when I made the motion that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration be now heard, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce was trying to get the floor to make his motion, that it caused consternation for a moment. MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
