subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several of the members on this side of the house who have taken part in this debate have expressed their distaste for doing so on the basis of personal friendship with the Speaker. I cannot claim to have an intimate friendship with the Speaker although our relations in this house and outside it have always been the best. As a preface to the remarks I wish to make today I should like to point out that I was one of those who, not so very long ago, rose in this house on a question of privilege in order to defend the Speaker when I considered that a report in one of the newspapers erroneously reported what he had said on an important occasion. I stand by every word I said at that time because the address which I heard him deliver on that occasion was, in my opinion, an excellent one and one which could not have been interpreted in any sense as being partisan. It was on that basis that I rose to defend Mr. Speaker and because we on this side of the house-as are hon. members, I am sure, on all sides of the house-are very jealous of the position of the Speaker with regard to impartiality. That is the reason why all of us, I am sure, take part in this debate; but we do not do so with any great alacrity because we know we are debating a motion which expresses lack of confidence in the Chair.
I wish first to draw attention to some of the remarks made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). In my opinion the minister made an excellent address from a partisan point of view. But in a debate in which partisanship is the least desirable of all ingredients, I regret to say that his contribution was not of his usual best. He made quite a point of quoting with approval the remarks of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) when that member spoke earlier in this debate. I am not at this point going to express my own opinion of that particular contribution. I would rather call on an independent opinion, from a source which-because of the fact that the writer is not a member of this house-could probably be depended upon to be non-partisan. I refer to the Winnipeg Free Press, a newspaper which is not notoriously unfriendly to this government. Here is what they have to
House of Commons
say with regard to exactly the same point. I quote from their editorial:
The three party leaders-Mr. St. Laurent, Mr. Drew and Mr. Coldwell-are all to be congratulated for their handling on Monday of the debate concerning the Speaker. (Mr. Quelch. for the Social Credit party, made a nasty speech; but its inappropriateness to the occasion is merely an additional sign that the Social Credit philosophy is without understanding or care for the principles of parliamentary democracy.)

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: It was the truth he stated.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my regret is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, by quoting with approval what is referred to in this editorial, has placed himself in the same category of being without understanding or care for the principles of parliamentary democracy, in the view of the Winnipeg Free Press.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: If that is true, so has Mr. Speaker Brand.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I do not think that remark is going to take away anything from what I have just said. I feel it is unfortunate that, in a situation of this kind, the government should be trying to leave the impression, in their so-called defence of the Speaker, that the members on the opposite side of the house are attacking the Speaker for partisan purposes. That is not the case.
In his address the minister said that the members on this side of the house-particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-had tried to get at the government through the Speaker. I suggest that the very reverse is the fact, namely that the government got at the opposition through the Speaker and that they are the ones who caused this whole mess. Not only will members of this house who were eyewitnesses to the whole of these events confirm that point of view. After all, the newspapers of this country, for the most part,- particularly on the question of procedure- are not taking a partisan point of view but are trying to call the shots as they see them. One has only to look through the newspapers these days to see that there has been a long procession of opinion in which it has been plainly stated that the government is responsible for having undermined the authority and the dignity of the Chair in the debate which has just ended.
Now, with the preponderance of evidence and opinion on the part of disinterested persons outside this house, I think it would have been better for the government to have admitted its mistake at this point and in that way to have salvaged the dignity and decorum of the Chair, rather than try to

House of Commons
place the responsibility on the other side of the house. I am quite happy to support what I have just said by a further quotation from the same newspaper. On the editorial page of the June 4 issue under the title, "Mr. Speaker", I find this:
That Mr. Speaker Beaudoin should be a casualty of the pipe line debate at Ottawa is more than a personal tragedy. It is also a political disaster.
Then they go on to say:
It is that which makes the personal tragedy of the censure motion on the Mr. Speaker so acute.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: From what is the hon. gentleman reading?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
From an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press of June 4, 1956. I continue:
Unfortunately, the painfulness of the tragedy does not lessen the hard reality of the political disaster. No opposition could have failed, in the circumstances of last Friday, to declare its loss of confidence in the Speaker and move censure on him.
Then farther on they say:
The government thought that a bulldozer was the right instrument to clear the path of the pipe line bill and learned too late that the result was in fact a chaos and bitterness in which probably no Speaker could achieve what parliament requires of him, because parliament is not meant to function this way.
Those are strong and unequivocal words. They do not beat about the bush. They place the responsibility squarely on the shoulders of the government where, in my opinion, it belongs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Why take it out on the Speaker then?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman who has just asked that question, what other way an opposition could register a protest under those circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: By a vote of want of confidence in the government, of course.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
That, I am afraid, would be much too late because the Speaker has already been crucified by the government.
It is not my intention to review the events which led up to this censure motion, the points of order and procedure that took place on last Thursday and Friday, because that has been thoroughly done in this debate. The experts on both sides of the house have already put that on the record and I wish merely to make this reference in that regard. If there is any doubt in the minds of members opposite as to the role that has been played by those who took an active part in the procedural debates in this house I would refer them to an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal a few days ago. The whole

editorial was devoted to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) but out of respect for his modesty I will not quote it. One has only to read that editorial to realize that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre deserved better at the hands of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) than he received today. It is quite clear the hon. member was fighting for a principle that is vital to the functioning of this parliament and that has been recognized by the press right across this country, not by a press that is friendly to the party to which he belongs but by a press that recognizes genius and ability when it sees it.
The matter which I shall discuss particularly today is not a question of technicalities or procedure but rather more in a philosophical vein concerning what I regard to be the greatest error made by members sitting behind the government. What the government itself has done has been well laid on the record already. I contend that the rank and file of members who support the government have the primary responsibility because it is by their grace that the government holds power. It is their attitude to which I wish to draw the attention of the house, and which I think resulted in the tragedy we have seen.
I want to refer to the address made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George on May 29 in which he, while talking on a point of order, placed on the record the quotation from section 49 of the British North America Act. One sentence in the quotation is this:
Questions arising in the House of Commons shall be decided by a majority of voices . . .
Now, he proceeded from there to argue that because of section 49 of the British North America Act the majority shall always decide. He fell into a trap that is often the result of over-simplicity. The same argument was taken up later by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert) and some other members supporting the government in which they insisted that it is the duty and the right of the majority to rule. If one were to follow that to its logical conclusion, we would have the most vicious type of one-party government in this country that could ever be envisaged. It would come, in my opinion, very close to the theory set out by Karl Marx in which he argued for the dictatorship of the proletariat on the basis of the fact there was more of the proletariat than any other class and therefore that class shall rule and the rights of the other people shall be taken away. In other words, it is rule by majority, by brute strength. We cannot subscribe, we cannot even entertain, such a thought in this parliament or in this country.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman deny that section 49 of the British North America Act is in existence now?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
What the hon. member read into the record was the main part of section 49. I think that was the only part he did put on the record, that questions arising in the House of Commons shall be decided on a majority of voices. I do not quite get the point of his question. Certainly, I do not deny the British North America Act is in existence. Unless the hon. member meant to ask something else, I am not quite sure how to answer. There is no debate about that. Section 49 of the British North America Act does exist and it does say what the hon. member put on the record. I am not questioning the accuracy of his quotation. All I am pointing out is what he and others who spoke as he did took that quotation to mean and the implication that carries with it.
The standing orders of this house are the British North America Act of the House of Commons. We are talking about minority rights. I am not particularly concerned about the minority in this House of Commons, which is the opposition. We are probably a less vulnerable minority than any in the country because in this house we are in a fluid position. The minority of today may be the majority of tomorrow. We are in a position to speak up for ourselves and make a protest when we see the rights of the minority in this house being trampled upon. Therefore, I am not particularly concerned as to what happens to members of the opposition in this House of Commons, but I am very much concerned about the philosophic acceptance of the philosophy, with all its implications, that the majority shall rule. If we accept that as a philosophy and apply it, particularly in a country such as ours where, as a matter of fact speaking from the point of view of our population in this country we are a nation of minorities, there is no telling what may happen.
With respect to racial origin, there is no group in this country that has a majority. We are a nation of minorities, and if we ever allow ourselves to follow the implications of the arguments presented by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Richardson), the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert), and others who have spoken on that side of the house, that the majority shall rule, it is their right to do so, then we shall be heading for very serious trouble,
House of Commons
much more serious than that which we have witnessed in the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I would not like to interrupt the hon. member, I do not propose to do so unless he permits it. May I ask another question? Does the hon. member now propose, either in this session or in some early session, to move an amendment so that section 49 of the British North America Act will be changed?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: There was never any question about that.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the hon. member is serious in asking that question. I think the content of the question itself indicates that he is not expecting an answer.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I am.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Certainly, I have no intention of moving that that section of the act be taken out; in the first place because I see no reason for removing it, and in the second place because it is not this House of Commons that would amend the act, anyway, it would be the British House of Commons.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask a question? What does the hon. member understand it to mean when section 49 says that questions shall be decided by a majority of voices? What does he understand that to mean?

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I am glad that question was asked, because it brings me exactly to the point I was about to make, Mr. Speaker, namely, that in the acceptance of a majority decision we must remember that it has to be applied and understood on the basis of rules and laws. If we applied the bare theory that the majority shall rule, without taking into consideration the rules under which they shall operate, or the laws of the land under which they shall operate, then we would find ourselves in an impossible position. Let me put it this way. Suppose we applied that theory in its bare implications to a court of law and said that the majority in court shall decide. Then, of course, we would not have justice. We operate in courts of law under certain laws and they are applied according to the way they are interpreted by the presiding judge. It is not a question of who has more lawyers in court; it is not a question of the jury being composed of 12 and the accused only one person and therefore he has automatically to lose the case. The laws are interpreted and adhered to strictly, and that is exactly what has to be done in this house. The standing orders of this house are the British North America Act of the House of Commons, and the moment the government

House of Commons
decides that the standing orders are a mere obstacle in its path and begins to find ways of circumventing those standing orders and the rules of this house, at that point it is abusing section 49 of the British North America Act and not using it. That is the point exactly. The rules of this house provide for certain procedures; they provide for the way in which legislation shall be brought forward step by step; they provide for points of order, questions of privilege and so on. I contend, sir, it is not the Speaker's responsibility nor his right to concern himself with the speed or effectiveness with which legislation passes through this house. That, I contend, is the responsibility of the members of this house. The Speaker's responsibility and function are strictly to interpret the rules as they are and to treat with fine impartiality all members on both sides of the house.
As the very controversial debate proceeded, one could perhaps draw this type of analogy from what happened. Here we were on a very controversial bill. The government was presenting its side of the argument and the opposition its side of the argument. It was something like a see-saw based on a fulcrum. At one point the government felt that the opposition perhaps was placing arguments that were more weighty and the see-saw began to come down in favour of the opposition. It was at that point that the Speaker moved the fulcrum and that is what started this whole controversy so far as the Speaker is concerned. At the point at which the seesaw was finely balanced, when the weight of the argument on each side was particularly heavy and the slightest shift of the fulcrum made a great difference as to the outcome of that controversy, at that point the Speaker shifted the fulcrum in favour of the government. I am not going to go into the question of why he did so; I am not going to go into all the details of how he did so. That is already on record. But the fact remains, and it is unanswerable, that the Speaker shifted the fulcrum in favour of the government at a very crucial point in the debate. Because that was done and because it was done contrary to the rules of this house, the opposition had no other recourse than to do what it eventually did, and therefore the motion is before the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the statements that I am about to make, the discussion of this motion will terminate and we shall then deal with this matter in one of two ways. I shall come back later to the ways in which this can be dealt with.
When I spoke first on the introduction of this motion I made it clear it was with the utmost reluctance and with very deep regret that we found it necessary to introduce a motion of this kind against a Speaker for whom,

as I said on that occasion, we have had not only respect but personal affection.
Since I presented that motion a number of speeches have been made; three have been made by members of the government. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has spoken, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has spoken, and today we heard from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). If there had been any uncertainty before about the necessity for a motion of this kind that uncertainty would have been removed by the nature of the speeches which have been made by the members of the government.
The Prime Minister washed his hands of all responsibility. Not only did he wash his hands of any personal responsibility but he imputed to the opposition motives which indeed would have made us unworthy to sit as members of this house if they had been true. I challenged the statements of the Prime Minister at that time but instead of withdrawing from his position he reemphasized it. The Prime Minister had this to say, as reported at page 4657 of Hansard:
This situation will appear to many, in spite of the elevated tone of the addresses made in the house this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and by the leader of the C.C.F. party, as being one more attempt to prevent the majority in parliament from reaching a point where it would be entitled to vote upon the propriety or otherwise of this controversial measure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must intervene on a question of privilege. I think it is a most improper suggestion that a matter brought forward in this way should in any way be suggested as a means of delaying debate in the pipe line proceedings.
I then went on to say:
I repudiate any suggestion of that kind and greatly regret that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) would have thought of making such a suggestion.
To that the Prime Minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, not even the Prime Minister could avoid thinking that each and every move that has been made since the pipe-line resolution was first brought before the house was designed to prevent it from reaching a point where it might become a statute of the Canadian parliament.
That was the position taken by the Prime Minister. We were dealing with a most unusual situation. We were dealing with a situation in no way correctly interpreted by the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Health and Welfare. We were dealing with an unqualified decision by the Speaker a week ago Thursday night to accept a motion which he in fact had suggested in form and assisted in drafting; and then the following morning without notice, without authority, without precedent
House of Commons
of any kind, he rose in this place to say he had come to the conclusion that he had made a mistake.
Mr. Speaker, if there was any uncertainty about the decision the night before it was the duty of one member of the government, whoever it might be, to raise that question. The members of the government were not caught by surprise. It was apparent they knew what was going to be done; it was evident. It was equally evident when the organized applause started immediately upon the announcement by the Speaker of what he was doing. Had they not known they would not have realized the significance of the decision which had been made.

This was no ordinary decision.
Then we had the Minister of Finance washing his hands of responsibility and making the unctuous suggestion that he had sought as no one else had to prevent the disturbances. The Minister of Finance now nods his head in support of that statement. The Minister of Finance sat here without a comment while the organized bedlam that is recorded in Hansard was carried forward by hon. members opposite largely under the direction of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill).

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance had this to say, as reported at page 4683 of Hansard:
I am going to say something that is rather difficult for me to say under the circumstances. Both the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the C.C.F. this afternoon said that all of us ought to regret what has happened, particularly what happened on Friday. I am going to agree with both of them. However, I hope that in expressing agreement in that sense I am not to be taken as having accepted any responsibility for it.
Oh, Mr. Speaker, those words will go down in Hansard as the words of a man who put before the house one of the most tawdry pretences that has ever been heard in this chamber. Men who sat here heard the bedlam raised by the supporters of the government without a word of objection; then the minister is quite ready to agree that others are responsible; but, oh, not the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris). Listen to what he said, as reported on page 4684 of Hansard of June 4:
A week ago Thursday night I did what no other member who has spoken in this debate has done. I rose in my place and appealed to the followers on this side of the house to remain in a condition which would not excite any feelings in this house, and from that day to this they have done so.
Let anyone examine the pages of Hansard between the Thursday night to which he refers in the previous week and the time at which he spoke and the answer will be found to a sanctimonious statement of that kind, completely denied by the record for all time.
This subject was dealt with further today by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I would have hoped that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would have acted more in keeping with the reputation which he has deserved of respecting accuracy and the responsibilities of this house. Again from him we heard a distortion of the record. That is a shameful thing as it stands permanently embedded in Hansard for years to come. He said:
I am not misled by this resolution.
No, he was not misled by the resolution. Then, even worse, he went on to say: "In their eager desire to try to force on the people an unnecessary election which will not resolve this question, some of my hon. friends opposite care not, Samsonlike, if they pull

down the Speaker's chair and the pillars of parliament along with it."
The simile may not have been inappropriate. It will be recalled that the temple which was torn down was a temple of evil men. It was a temple of the Philistines, not a temple of freedom like this House of Commons. It may be worth recalling also that Samson in that ultimate act of despair used his strength to relieve himself from the chains which bound him, Yes, the simile may not have been inappropriate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: He was defeated too.

subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: He destroyed his enemies.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The Minister of National Health and Welfare says, "He was defeated too." In that single remark the Minister of National Health and Welfare condemns this whole government. That is his estimate of their attitude toward this situation; it was not whether Samson was rightly chained or not; the people that had the power, according to him, had the right, and the man who tore down the evil things, according to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, lost too. I do not believe there is one hon. member on this side of the house who has been expressing his opinion in regard to this unhappy incident who would not far rather lose in a decent and honourable cause than win by the sheer use of force to which the government has appealed on this occasion.
The government has been poorly served by those who have sought to divert attention from the issue before us. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) said that I had tried to argue in regard to the Speaker's ruling; that is not so. I had tried to be heard on a point of order, to point out that it was not the role of the Speaker to become counsel for the government and judge as well. I was denied a hearing, and so were other hon. members who sought to be heard.
Oh, we are told that when the Speaker is on his feet others cannot rise. That statement can only be made by those who do not know our rules or have not followed the proceedings in this house. Points of order are frequently raised while the Speaker is standing. If he deems it appropriate the Speaker resumes his seat and permits the point of order or the question of privilege, as the case may be, to be heard.
Unless it were possible for members to rise while the Speaker is standing, particularly when he is making some comment about the proceedings in this house, it would not be possible for any effective discussion of the rules of this house, and the procedure in this house, and the rights of members, to

take place. Certainly they have a right to rise while the Speaker is standing. It is true that they have not the right to rise to engage in an argument with the Speaker while he is standing. Nevertheless there is not an hon. member of this government or an hon. member opposite who has taken any part in the legitimate and proper debates of this house who has not seen many occasions where points of order or questions of privilege could be raised only by the person rising while the Speaker was standing. In that way the member indicates his intention to state the question -when the Speaker resumes his seat.
Let it be said that on most occasions in the past the Speaker has acceded without question to the demand to be heard on a point of order or a question of privilege. It was only on this black Friday that has just passed, when he had taken the unprecedented course first of all in acting on behalf of the government in presenting a proposal and second in passing judgment without permitting hon. members to be heard, that he denied to any hon. member in this house the right to be heard. In an affront, not to members of parliament but to the people of Canada, he rang a bell which could have been the death knell of freedom unless there had been members here who were prepared to stand up for their rights on that occasion.
As we all know, every decision of that kind becomes a precedent embedded in the records. What a dreadful precedent to have established on this occasion. The Minister of Finance, referring to my statement that there had been newspaper criticism outside of this house before it arose here, professed his ignorance of any such criticism. Within the rules of this house, it is not possible for me to use terms appropriate to such a statement. I cannot believe that the minister does not read the newspapers. I cannot believe that he was unaware of criticism which had been levelled against the Speaker and the Chairman for conduct which had already aroused the indignation of certain members of the government as well.
The minister sought to convey the impression that if there had been criticism outside it was criticism prompted by what was said by the members of the opposition. Let him point to a single case where that criticism had been directed to the subject of the widespread criticism that was coming from outside because of the manner in which debates were being conducted here under the lengthy admonitions of the Speaker, under the unnecessary repetition of precedents to support his position at times when no member of the government had raised any question at all. It was then that the criticism came from

House of Commons
outside, not from here. Even then we were prepared to hope that, as so often happens, this advice from outside might have its effect. Unfortunately, the Speaker did not heed the warnings.
The criticism that was made was not merely criticism as to the long and extraordinary statements being made by the Speaker; it was due to the fact that the Speaker was substituting himself for the government in raising issues which had not even been brought forward. That was the situation which finally came to a head.
Then the Minister of Finance has sought to interpret the statements made a week ago Thursday night as statements indicating that the Speaker was reserving his decision in regard to the admission of a motion which he himself had helped to frame and upon which debate had already taken place. There was no suggestion of any such thing. He had accepted the motion; he had emphasized the fact that before this house met he had already examined and carefully read one of the letters referred to by the hon. member for Nanaimo, who presented the motion, and that in his opinion this was not only a matter of privilege but of serious privilege. It was upon that basis that he accepted the motion.
May I make it clear? We are not speaking here about dissatisfaction with the Speaker's ruling. We are talking about the way in which the ruling was made. As I said in the opening remarks in support of this motion, we certainly would not present a motion of this kind simply because of what we thought had been a mistake on the part of the Speaker. What we were directing our criticism to was the way in which the Speaker made this ruling, and his conduct on Friday morning. That is the point that is before the house.
I know that it is not appropriate to quote newspaper editorials by way of argument in a manner that reflects upon the house. I would point out, however, that the Prime Minister and others who have spoken have used editorials, and to that extent I would certainly question the propriety of any denial at this time of the right to read an editorial or article relating to this subject. However, I shall qualify what I intend to say still more. I propose to read certain things that have appeared in the press, not as arguments but as an indication of what the impression is upon the minds of experienced observers. That is something which surely cannot be a matter which is of no concern to the members of this house.
Already reference has been made to an editorial appearing in the Winnipeg Free Press on Monday, June 4. I shall not repeat

House of Commons
that part which has already been read into the record. Whatever else may be said about the Winnipeg Free Press, it would not in the ordinary course of events be regarded as a newspaper whose leanings had been unduly toward the opposition. I should like to read that editorial simply to indicate what the attitude of responsible observers is in relation to what has taken place in this house, because, as I have already pointed out on an earlier occasion, this is the house of the people, and it is the people's rights that are at issue here. We as individuals are merely the servants of all those millions of Canadians whom collectively we represent on both sides of this house. In an editorial headed "Mr. Speaker", this is what the Winnipeg Free Press had to say on that occasion:
That Mr. Speaker Beaudoin should be a casualty of the pipe-line debate at Ottawa is more than a personal tragedy. It is also a political disaster.
The Canadian House of Commons has had few Speakers who have worked as hard and commanded such general respect as Mr. Beaudoin. The proper measure of him can be taken by asking this question: under how many Speakers would the House of Commons have got as far as it has, in the unprecedented circumstances of the pipeline debate, before the opposition was stirred to censure the Speaker? What if Mr. Beaudoin had not started out with a great fund of goodwill? What if the opposition had not previously learned to respect both his impartiality and his great knowledge of the rules and precedents of parliament? The government's handling of the pipe-line bill could readily have created yet more chaos and bitterness, even sooner in the parliamentary proceedings, than it has.
Respect for the Speaker is an essential lubricating oil in the functioning of parliament. When the machine is running so hot it is bound to burn some of that oil. The measure of Mr. Beaudoin's quality is that the asset was so large and survived rapid consumption for as long as it did.
It is that which makes the personal tragedy of the censure motion of the Speaker so acute. Unfortunately, the painfulness of the tragedy does not lessen the hard reality of the political disaster No opposition could have failed in the circumstances of last Friday, to declare its loss of confidence in the Speaker and move censure on him.
Then I omit the part that has already been read into the record and I continue reading from the same editorial:
Whether the Speaker was right or wrong in his first decision is open to prolonged discussion, of little public interest. But it is perfectly plain that, by changing his mind over night, so greatly to the government's advantage, the Speaker becomes exposed to opposition suspicion of having yielded to government pressure. The opposition is fully entitled to act on the basis that its confidence in the Speaker's impartiality is completely destroyed. And without that confidence, the normal proceedings of parliament are impossible.
Mr. Beaudoin in this is the unhappy victim of circumstances beyond his control. The government thought that a bulldozer was the right instrument to clear the path of the pipe line bill and learned too late that the result was in fact

a chaos and bitterness in which probably no Speaker could achieve what parliament requires of him, because parliament is not meant to function this way.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I wish just to refer to another article which is not an editorial. It is an article by a man who is generally regarded as one of the most competent reporters and observers associated with any newspaper in Canada. I refer to Mr. I. Norman Smith, whose rewards for the quality of his reporting have won for him an enviable reputation not only in the newspaper field but in the sphere of letters as well. Let me read just a short quotation from what he said in an article to which reference has already been made and which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of June 4 under the title "They Tore Up a Part of My National Pride". Let is be remembered that the writer of this article was writing not as an editorial writer detached from the scene but as a reporter who had been in parliament and who was in the House of Commons at the time the events in question occurred. I quote from that article:
Isn't it kinder to say that House Leader Harris was ignorant of what he was doing when several times he was so lacking in taste as to go up to the Speaker's chair and speak intently with that officer whose impartiality is anciently unapproachable? The Speaker and his rulings were under fire and question during all this time. Perhaps Mr. Harris wasn't giving him instructions; perhaps he was just asking where he was going for Christmas.
But surely Mr. Harris must have been ignorant of the fact that for him to discuss Christmas or anything else with the Speaker at that particular time was to sully the Speaker and parliament and himself beyond the belief of any citizen sensitive to what parliamentary democracy means? "Get out of there!" cried out a Conservative member, but Mr. Harris saw no wrong and felt no discomfort-a state explained only by ignorance of a fairly high order, for instinct and institution were alike revolted.
I hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) laughing. A man who had that indictment presented by one of the most competent reporters in this country who sat in the gallery and saw what happened here is strangely unworthy of his responsibilities in this house if he can laugh at such an indictment.
Mr. Speaker, there was no question about the fact that messages were being passed. There was not an hon. member who did not see them; not one. There was not an hon. member who was not conscious of the atmosphere on Thursday night. There certainly was not an hon. member on Friday morning who was not conscious that it was the will of the government which had prevailed.

speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I wish to read also the words of another reporter. Again this is not an

editorial. It is from a report by a man who once again can be properly said not to have been unduly influenced by his close association with the Conservative party. This is an article by Mr. Douglas Leiterman which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, June 2, under the title "An Axe Flailing at the Root of Human Rights". Mr. Leiterman is a member of the press gallery who had observed what took place here in this house, with an opportunity to see what took place which is perhaps not afforded to all hon. members. Let me quote from that report:
For you were witnessing not only the debasement of a proud and accomplished Speaker. Not only the irresponsibility of a sorely-tried opposition. Not only the indecent haste of a thoughtless government. You were witnessing the axe flailing at the root of human rights, and fear wrapped around you as you watched.
Mr. Speaker Beaudoin had ruled honestly, according to his lights, the night before. The opposition had outmanoeuvred him, so resourcefully and so successfully that the pipe line bill was dangerously delayed.
What happened, over night, no one will ever know. But from the opening Friday morning Mr. Speaker behaved like a man under the gun.
Then I pass over some part of the report and read this:
Then the whirlwind. The Speaker, in carefully memorized phrases, proposed that all Thursday night's proceedings be wiped out; that the house go back to where it was at 5.15 p.m. Thursday. Why? Because he had made a "serious mistake" in everything he had done after that hour. The house was thunderstruck. It was a preposterous proposition. "Why not", demanded a member, "go back to last week, or last year?"
Beaudoin wavered but Finance Minister Harris, alarmed at the Speaker's floundering, admonished him to get on with it. Stiffen your back, Rene, he said in effect. The Speaker stiffened.
Then I pass on to the closing paragraphs of this report written by Mr. Leiterman:
What mattered was not that it was unfair, but that it was unjust, and unconstitutional. Mr. Speaker followed the rules until they got in the government's way. Then, he threw the rule book in the Ottawa river and proclaimed: "Let the house decide". That could only mean, "let the government decide", since the government controls the house. The rules, whose purpose is to protect the rights of parliament, ceased to protect. The oligarchy could do what it would-and it did.
Mr. Speaker, I have read those extracts from three highly responsible newspapers written by very responsible men who are highly trained observers. I did so, as I said before, so that the hon. members in this house might be fully aware of what the impression is outside of this house. Others could be read as well, equally critical-

speechtext: Or to the contrary.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
-and equally damaging to the relationship between the Speaker and the
House of Commons
house, but above all equally revealing as to the relationship between the Speaker and the government.
In his solemn oath of office the Speaker has sworn to serve parliament, to serve all the members. It is upon that clear duty that our whole concept of the parliamentary system has grown through the centuries as a result of trial and error. Break that sense of service to the whole house and you not only deny the possibility of the Speaker properly performing his duties, but you shatter the relationship between the house and the Speaker without which orderly debate cannot proceed.
The Minister of Finance made much of the fact that there had been numerous appeals against this Speaker's rulings in recent days. He made much of the fact that there had been few appeals on earlier occasions. Yes, it is true. The reason for those appeals was because-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: MR. DREW    MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
-it was only in those recent weeks that it became apparent that Mr. Speaker was not accepting his responsibility to the whole house but that the government was imposing its will to meet a deadline imposed by strangers to this house. What right was it of theirs what date saw the termination of a legitimate discussion on a subject proclaimed by the government itself as one of the most important ever to come before this house? What right was it of anyone outside of this house to impose terms and tell us when we must conclude our proper discussions of the affairs of the people of Canada? The Speaker's rulings were appealed because the Speaker was no longer making rulings consistent with the rules presented only last year by a committee of which he had been chairman. The words of these rules, clear words not open to misinterpretation, were twisted and distorted in their meaning. Again, there might have been criticism but not condemnation of this man if the Speaker had merely made a mistake in the interpretation of these rules.
The significant thing was that the .misinterpretation of clear words, in English and in French, contained in those rules approved by this house served in every case the interests of the government in their demand that, no matter what happened, debate be terminated by a date that suited a United States controlled company about whose welfare they were so greatly concerned.
Today we heard a speech from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). Amongst other things he said the motion had not the slightest justification for presentation.

House of Commons
I have already read a statement made by a man who certainly would not be accused of any known sympathy for the Conservative party, except in this particular instance. May I at this point say that every Canadian should be proud of what has been said by the newspapers which have been openly associated with the Liberal party for many years. Never before in this country's history have we seen greater tribute to the real freedom of the press than has been expressed in relation to the incidents which have occurred in this house. We said at the outset of this debate that one of the reasons that we sought full opportunity to debate the measure that was before us in an orderly, unhampered way, was that one of the main functions of debate in this house was to shape public opinion outside through the thoughts and information gained from the press which reports what we do here.
We saw the valuable consequences of that relationship between the press and the public in the defence production debate last year. We saw the government finally bow, and graciously I concede, to the overwhelming demand of the people of Canada when they expressed opinions which were shaped and formed and reached by an examination of what they read in the press or heard over that other great medium of information, the radio. That was after weeks of debate. Unless every hon. member opposite felt that the Prime Minister had been wrong when he rose on the last day of that long debate last year and indicated what the government intended to do, then hon. members opposite should have been the first to say, "We wish to retain that evidence of democracy in action which we saw clearly expressed here in this house last year after the public had become informed as to what the facts actually were." The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) quoted a very great Speaker of the British House of Commons, Mr. Speaker Brand, seeking to justify the attitude of the Speaker in this house in refusing to hear anyone in regard to proceedings which he had undertaken on his own initiative, or rather on his own initiative so far as this house was concerned. The Minister of National Health and Welfare quoted Mr. Speaker Brand in this way: "I shall be justified if I refuse to call upon any more members to speak." What a difference, Mr. Speaker, what a difference between the two illustrations. There had been extended debate in the case when Mr. Speaker Brand made this decision; exercising the right he had as Speaker, he indicated he felt that he had heard enough in the debates that had already taken place in regard to the point of order that had been raised. It was only then, after hearing many speakers, that he said: "I shall be justified if I refuse to call 
upon any more members to speak." In this case, these words are not applicable. The Speaker, with no motion before him, with no pretence of a motion, because he cannot make a motion, and with no suggestion of a debate, because he is not allowed to participate in debate, made a decision contrary to every precedent and then refused, not to hear any more members, but to hear any members at all even to the extent of a single word.
This was no ordinary refusal. It was the effect of what he did that must be examined in considering the motion now before us. The effect of what he did was to remove the first roadblock in the way of the government's steamroller. There was still another. The other roadblock related to proceedings which had taken place between 5.15 of the day before and the time we met on Friday morning. It was necessary to remove that second roadblock. Then, the Speaker proceeded with something that has no precedent here or in any other parliamentary institution. Not a word had been said by any member of the government suggesting that this be done on that Friday morning. Nevertheless, the Speaker rose and said that he was going to put a proposal before us. That proposal was to strike out, for all practical purposes, everything that had happened between 5.15 on Thursday and the time we met on Friday morning. As it has been aptly described in the press, it became the day that never was. We then reverted by an unprecedented procedure to 5.15 the day before. Yes, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare has said, we can all make mistakes; we all do- that is, except the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. We all make mistakes. There would have been no serious objection if the Speaker had made a mistake. It was not the fact that there had been a mistake; it was the obvious purpose of that unprecedented action which we could not ignore, as has been so properly pointed out by the Winnipeg Free Press.
We would be derelict in our duty as members of the opposition, Mr. Speaker-might I go further and say hon. members opposite are derelict in their duty if they are unwilling to recognize the need for the restoration of the authority, the traditions and the responsibility of this house in a manner in keeping with the seriousness of what occurred. By that weird device for which there is to be found nowhere in any record even the pretence of a precedent, the second road block was removed and the steamroller moved on to its stated objective and the time limit set by those outside this house.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, in quoting Mr. Speaker Brand, said, "If

that is not the most classical justification of the course followed by the Speaker I do not know where it could be found." There is not even the slightest hint of a similarity; there is not even the slightest hint of a suggestion. When the Speaker did raise the question of delay on Thursday night it was not delay- and the minister knows it-in regard to a ruling on the motion. He sought delay so that he could prepare a statement as to his position in relation to the example of what he regarded as serious prejudice. He had made his finding. He had not merely stated that he had read the letter; he said that it was a question of privilege and a most serious question of privilege. I am not going to argue as to whether he was right or wrong the night before. As has been pointed out, that is utterly unimportant. He had made his decision. The house had become seized of this matter and he had no right of any kind to withdraw that from the house. Certainly, he had no right to do so without hon. members being in a position to argue as to the merits of that course. It was not a case of arguing with the ruling; it was a case of dealing in appropriate terms with our rights. That, the Speaker refused. I repeat, the refusal must be examined in relation to its effect and not merely as an ordinary mistake.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, for some reason in regard to which I am not clear, and I fancy no hon. member in this house is very clear about it, sought to convey the impression that I had introduced closure in the Ontario legislature. I moved the previous question. The Minister of National Health and Welfare knows perfectly well that the previous question has been moved frequently in this house. It was moved by the Minister of Finance last year in the defence production debate.
The Minister of Finance will recall that on that occasion there were a great many speeches after that motion had been put. The previous question does not deny debate; the previous question is merely a devise to prevent debate on other matters coming before the house before a vote is taken, that is all, and the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and Welfare are well aware of that affect. The previous question permits debate to proceed in its normal manner. The previous question permits debates of the full length permitted by the rules of this house, not the limited debates of 20 minutes which are imposed under the closure motion.
Yes, I moved the previous question in Ontario; but the Minister of National Health and Welfare did not have to go to Ontario. I have moved the previous question here in
House of Commons
this house; so have ministers of the crown on a number of occasions. It is something very different; and if that is the best evidence of any inconsistency on our part I would suggest that a little more research be done on this question.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare implied that there was something shameful about bringing this extraordinary situation to the attention of the house. These were the minister's words, or certainly the context of his words: What is shameful is that the members of this house will be called upon to make a decision. Well, I have already suggested to the Prime Minister a way by which he can avoid that decision which the Minister of National Health and Welfare regards as shameful. What is shameful about dealing with the destruction of the rules and traditions and practices and the established procedure of this house?
The Minister of National Health and Welfare referred to my statement that there had been criticism outside. He said that I had indicated there had been rumblings long before the debate arose. Yes, I am sure the minister is well aware of the criticism to which I referred. That was not related directly to any criticism in this house; it was related to the opinion of competent observers with regard to the proceedings which had taken place here, something that is not only the right but the duty of the press of this country, a free land.
Then the Minister of National Health and Welfare used words that should not be overlooked. He said that he did not know what standard of fairness prompted this course of slander by smear. If he wants to speak about shame, then let me say that is one of the most shameful statements I have ever heard in this house.

House of Commons
The Minister of National Health and Welfare says that the very wording of the resolution is justification for not accepting it. The wording in the simplest and most moderate form describes exactly what took place here in this house last Friday, as the record will unfortunately show for just as long as the Hansard records of this house are read.
The minister asked, is reversal of a decision by the Speaker justification for such a motion? Is refusal to hear the members justification for this motion? No, and we never suggested that. What we have said and what I say now is that it was the reversal of a decision on his own initiative and without any precedent while at the same time refusing to hear any member of the opposition with regard to what he was doing. That is what we have said and that is what I say now.
The situation now before us is one which can be dealt with by this house. It is also one which can be dealt with by the government. This was no mere question of mistake. I said at the very outset we would never have thought of a motion of this kind that dealt only with a mistake in a ruling. I have indicated what was the impression of experienced reporters who observed this scene clearly, after they had witnessed the events of a week ago Thursday night and last Friday morning.
This is something that goes to the root of our continuing ability as members of a parliament with a government and an opposition. This is something that goes to the root of our ability to serve the people of Canada effectively here in this chamber. There can be a vote on a strictly partisan basis, as was indicated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I do not agree with him in that assessment. I do not agree this will be on a strictly partisan basis. I believe, however, it will be a vote which if it is taken, will divide this house in a manner that is wholly inconsistent with the relationship of the Speaker to the house if he is to serve the house as a whole.
As a minority we are not claiming the right or the ability to impose our will upon the government; nevertheless, in the most earnest terms I could employ I sought at the time I introduced this motion to impress upon the Prime Minister that something ugly has come into this house, that the relationship of hon. members to each other, the relationship of hon. members to the Chair, and the traditions, decency and standards of this house are all affected by what has occurred. I said then and I repeat now as I close these remarks that this parliament cannot be the same again. A government which was


prepared to do what was done at the close of this house a week ago last Thursday and the opening on Friday morning, a government which is prepared to defend this action with the specious arguments we have heard, cannot again command that measure of confidence in this house which a government should command no matter what party may form it.
There will not again be a return to that easy relationship and mutual understanding which with all our differences is essential to the performance of our duties, until the people of Canada, whose house this is, have an opportunity to choose the members, which will be done with the full knowledge by those people of all that has occurred in this house. If that were done a new parliament might well start in with that relationship which is so necessary. What has happened unfortunately cannot be forgotten. A new parliament, however, need not be hampered by the unhappy precedents which have been established in these past few days.
The Prime Minister has it within his power to restore the dignity of parliament by assuring the house now that at an appropriate time which will permit him to attend the conference in London and to carry out the necessary duties of government in the meantime, he will dissolve this house and seek from the people a mandate for a new parliament to bring parliament itself into harmony with the will of the people. If the Prime Minister would do that then I am sure there would be ready acceptance on this side of the proposal that this debate be adjourned.

It is the government in the course it has followed that has led by one inevitable step after another to this unhappy position. Let the government deal with this in the way it should. In that way it can avoid the necessity of a division upon this motion, but not otherwise.
I hope the government will accept its responsibilities in a sense of duty to the people of Canada, whose servants we are, and to future generations of Canadians whose happiness, whose opportunities, and whose welfare will be determined by what we do here.
