devoted officers of the Department of Fisheries who have done such a good job in conserving and developing our fisheries resources. The criticism will be a spur to me, as minister, to correct those things that hon. members feel should be improved upon.
Almost all the members who spoke touched on two or three main issues so far as fisheries were concerned. First and foremost was the matter of unemployment insurance for fishermen. This, of course, is a matter under my colleague the Minister of Labour, but my two colleagues the minister from Newfoundland, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the minister from Nova Scotia, the Minister of Public Works, as well as myself, are keenly interested and hopeful that a way can be found to include the fishermen of Canada under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
We have an interdepartmental committee working on this problem, and I think we have made quite good progress. I think it is fair to say that there would not be too much difficulty in bringing the British Columbia fishermen under the present act, mainly because British Columbia fishing is governed by fixed seasons, the length of which is set by the Department of Fisheries. So long as it is the intention not to pay unemployment insurance during the fishing season but merely for those who are unemployed outside the fishing season, it would not be too difficult.
It is a much more difficult problem in the maritime areas, where the major fisheries do not have fixed seasons. But we are hopeful we can come up with a satisfactory solution. We had a very helpful meeting with the officials of the big fishermen's unions on the west coast, who put forward their views on this matter.
The second matter discussed by almost every member from a coastal fishing riding was the matter of territorial waters. Almost all members seemed to agree with the fishermen and the fishing industry that the present three-mile limit is inadequate so far as conservation of our fisheries resources is concerned. The Fisheries Council of Canada and the fishermen's unions of Canada have supported an extension to at least 12 miles out, based on a straight base line drawn along our coast. As you know, this fall this whole problem is going to be the subject of a formal discussion at the United Nations, at which the Secretary of State for External Affairs will put forward the case which has been prepared.
The maritime members spoke about the very difficult problem of trawlers. The member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings especially raised it. The complaint results from the

fact that we keep our own Canadian trawlers, our big ships, 12 miles out to sea and so preserve the 12-mile coastal zone for fishermen who use smaller boats, draggers and even smaller, so there will be no interference between the big ships and the smaller ships. Unfortunately, however, we have no way of preventing foreign trawlers from coming into the three-mile limit since that is our present territorial boundary. We do not have that problem in British Columbia or in Newfoundland; it is a maritime provinces problem. It is a very difficult thing to decide because of the fact the inshore fishermen are vociferous about keeping the big ships out so they have a fair chance at the inshore fisheries, and naturally the Canadian trawlers who are 12 miles out and who see Spanish, Portuguese and other foreign trawlers inside that limit feel a sense of injustice.
In Nova Scotia they had a royal commission on this question, and our present policy is pretty well based on the findings of that commission. I cannot see that there is any clear-cut opinion in the fishing industry of Nova Scotia today for a change in the present regulations. We hope that a satisfactory conclusion will be a change in the territorial waters which will keep foreign trawlers out. This of course will be dependent on the United Nations discussions this fall.
One other question which almost every member raised was the need for more public works in the fishing ridings; anchorages, wharves or floats. This, of course, comes under my colleague the Minister of Public Works. I do the best I can in putting forward these requests from the fishermen for improved facilities. The entire assets of most fishermen are tied up in their fishing boats and gear, so naturally they want to see these things protected as much as possible.
Turning from these general questions raised by almost every member to other questions raised by members, I think the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, who led off in the debate, spoke with pride of the value of the fishing industry to Canadians. It amounts to over $200 million a year in market value. I heartily agree with him that it is a very important industry. It is a very scattered industry. I have calculated that there are over 40 constituencies where the fishing industry is an important industry. It is a great resource which we in Canada have done our best to husband, and I think we can look forward to a steadily increasing fishing industry in this country.
He and other maritime members emphasized the importance of not forgetting the importance of the cured fish and the salt-cured

industry of the maritime provinces. It is quite true we have had a very important development in the fresh and frozen fish industry, especially in fish sticks, and that is an added strength. I agree there is always going to be a need for a sound industry in the salted and cured fish of the maritimes. We are doing our best to encourage it. We do think it will be helpful to have a more diversified fishing industry, and not be totally dependent on markets in the Caribbean and Mediterranean.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni raised a question of why we do not make more use of our herring as human food. We have a very large catch of herring. This season on the west coast we caught an all-time record of a quarter of a million tons, and our east coast catch added to that, which means that about one-third of our fisheries catch in Canada is herring. Less than 2 per cent of the west coast herring is used for food. There is a larger percentage of the east coast herring used in that way, but we do put more than 90 per cent of our herring into fish meal and oil through reduction plants. This is not lost as a food resource, because these are the principal ingredients of the things which are added to food for our cattle and poultry, and they have resulted in improvement in growth and size.
The fishermen's union of British Columbia asked me to visit Norway on my way to Russia last summer to see what the Norwegians were doing with their herring. They felt that there was a much greater use being made of herring. So I made inquiries, and found to my surprise that over 80 per cent of Norwegian herring is also made into fish meal and fish oil, so the answer is the same in both countries. Herring is a small and bony fish, and the actual labour needed to fillet herring for the market and put it in a form acceptable to the modern housewife makes the cost so high that it is no longer competitive with other fish foods. We do not lose the value of herring as fish food in using it the way we do. We certainly would like to encourage the development of other uses for herring. At the moment it seems the principal use is going to be for fish meal and fish oil.
The hon. member asked me about our scientific program in the north Pacific. Last year the Americans, the Japanese and ourselves covered the entire treaty area of the north Pacific with the first real hydrographic and fisheries survey. We gained a lot of knowledge last summer. We shall have 25 ships out there this summer, all helping in the work of trying to find out the migration routes of the salmon, trying to find out the exact dividing line between those salmon which return to
Supply-Fisheries
our shores and those salmon which go to Siberian and Japanese streams. I was very much surprised last year to see the extent of the scientific work done by the Russians in their part of the Pacific. They are sending two of their scientists to the meeting of the north Pacific commission in Seattle this year, who will make a contribution in that field.
The hon. member also mentioned the difficulty between our Russian friends and our Japanese friends in the north Pacific last summer. Last month the Japanese and the Russians had a meeting in Moscow and agreed on a conservation treaty in the north Pacific, and have so stated. We have not yet got the particulars of it, but I am told it pretty well follows the pattern of our own three-nation north Pacific treaty.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni also raised the question of the spawning forecast issued by our department, which would seem to indicate that we had lost quite a heavy brood of salmon eggs because of the floods in British Columbia last fall. That is so. It was an act of God about which we can do very little, but we have had very encouraging reports this spring. Our scientists have noticed the greatest seaward migration of sockeye salmon from the Adams river in all our history.
He asked whether Indians were eligible for loans under the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act. That is a matter for decision pretty well by the bank managers. Indians are protected by law in many ways against being sued. Many of them have no real assets. Those who cannot obtain loans under this act, of course, have still the resources of the Indian affairs branch, wh'ch can make direct loans to Indians.
Then he asked what we were going to do when the great blast at Ripple Rock takes place to remove that obstacle to navigation. It will be at a time when the migratory fish, salmon and herring, are at a minimum. That is when the blast is scheduled to take place. There are no great numbers of ground fish in that area, mainly because the tidal sweep is so strong that ground fish do not hold their place. No doubt there will be some ground fish killed by the tremendous blast that will take place. They will come to the surface, and I am sure my hon. friend's constituents will be out there quickly to salvage as many of them as they can.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo commented on the place of the salt cod industry in Newfoundland, and indicated that the new plans were not the sole answer. He commented on the salt assistance program. He said it was a good program, but that the fishermen were required to fill out a form

Supply-Fisheries
which only a chartered accountant or a Rhodes scholar could understand. I am not a chartered accountant but I am the other. I must confess that I would have very great difficulty in filling out this form. Because of his observation I have given instructions to our officials to try to simplify this form for the benefit of the fishermen of the Atlantic provinces.
The hon. member for Nanaimo spoke of the great importance of fisheries in our history. In fact he said it was the search for fisheries that led to the discovery of Canada. In reading the recent biography of Sir John A. Macdonald I was impressed with how important the fisheries debates were in this house in the early days of our confederacy, and the negotiations in Washington between the United States and Britain which affected our fisheries, at which we were only bystanders. We have fortunately improved that situation since that day.
Then he raised a question which was novel to me, on the rights of the Indians in the Cowichan river with respect to their weirs. I had never heard of the weirs, but I found that our Indians up to 1939 did have their weirs on the side of the river, which was the only place in British Columbia where such weirs existed. It was in 1939 discussed at a meeting between the Indian band and the department and they agreed to abandon the weirs in return for the permission to use dip nets, spears and gaffs, which they have done quite satisfactorily.
Last season was a very poor season for chum salmon. It was a low run and some Indians had difficulty getting the number of salmon they usually get for food purposes for themselves, so blamed it on the lack of weirs. There is practically no limit on what Indians can take or how they take them as long as the salmon is for themselves or for their dogs.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich raised a point that he was very much bothered about, namely my refusal to accept the recommendations made by the international salmon commission that part of the Canadian fisheries area be completely closed. I gave the reasons why I had to do that at that time. Since that time the salmon commission have framed other regulations which are in keeping with the treaty passed in this house. I feel, from talking to members of the commission, that they think the time may be ripe to suggest changes in the treaty which, of course, will have to come before this parliament and the United States congress.
He raised one point which was very important to the work of our department. He

turned to me and said that I should look at the beam in my own eye, because he felt our fisheries officers were not being paid enough. That is a feeling I have, too. I was glad to have his observations, because at that time I was conducting a very strenuous campaign with the chairman of the civil service commission about the status of our officers as compared with other departments. It was a battle which I am glad to say I won, and I thank him for his comments which I was able to show as being illustrative of the fact that on both sides it was believed there was need for remedy there.
We have, of course, a problem in British Columbia because of the higher wage rates in effect in industry there as compared with the maritime provinces. We have uniform pay rates for our fisheries officers across the country. I think in the maritimes this pay is quite attractive in comparison with industrial pay, but in British Columbia there are many who feel that they can make more money in industry or in fishing itself rather than accepting employment as fisheries officers.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam raised the matter of our price support action a couple of years ago on bloaters from the Magdalen islands. He pointed out that we had sent salt cod to Korea and Greece, and that instead of condemning these bloaters and putting them into fish meal we should have sent them to the Congo or some depressed area. It is quite true we provided almost $1 million worth of salt cod after the earthquake in Greece and the war in Korea, but both these countries asked for salt cod. Salt fish is a staple of their diet.
These particular bloaters were a part of a very big catch in 1953. Bloaters have a very limited market. They are a very simple form of fish, a herring slightly salted and smoked whole. There is a limited market for them in Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The private industry had sold all their bloaters, but the co-operatives down there had held out for a market increase. There was a great drop in the market and they were unable to sell the bloaters without help for almost a year, and finally they asked for a price support.
Our price support program only relates to the fishermen themselves. We examined these bloaters. Those unfit for human consumption were destroyed. There were some not unfit for human consumption but they could not be sold to anybody because they were stiff and hard and crumbled into powder when touched. These we got at a very low price and turned over to the fish plant to be reduced

into fish meal. I do not think the people in Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Greece or Korea would have welcomed the bloaters, and the cost of transporting them there certainly would have been far more than the worth of the bloaters.
The hon. member for Charlotte raised the question of the suggested move of two sections of the St. Andrews research station to Halifax. The hon. member for Royal also raised the question. Since it has been before the house I have asked the fisheries research board to hold up any action on that proposal. I have appointed as an industrial member of the research board from New Brunswick the manager of one of the fish plants in Charlotte, Mr. Leigh Williamson, who is also the mayor of the city of St. Andrews, and I am sure he will put forward the reasons against making any alterations at the next meeting of the research board.
I think those are the major points that were raised on item 1. There are a number of other matters directly connected with other items, such as the vessel indemnity plan, which I think probably could be best answered on those items.

Mr. Chairman, I have just one question at the moment. The minister has referred to the problem of territorial waters. We realize this is a serious problem, one which has been before this committee now for several years, and which I am sure will be before it for some years yet to come.
When I raised the matter last year and asked the minister particularly with respect to the Curtis report which was to be submitted to the government, I think the record shows the answer I got at that time was that this report had not yet been studied by the government but it would be shortly and thereafter the report of the Curtis commission would be made available. I may be mistaken about this, but as far as I know the report has not yet been made available. I was wondering where that report is and if it now could be produced so we could study the situation further.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The report has been completed. It is in the Department of External Affairs. I do not know whether my colleague has prepared his submission to the United Nations for this fall, but I do not know of any reason why the actual Curtis report should not be made available. I have told my colleague of the undertaking I gave here in the house, and I am sure the report will be made available.

I hope the minister will take this matter up with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because we were told 67509-309
Supply-Fisheries
last year it was in his hands and certainly this matter is going to go on for some considerable time. It seriously affects some constituencies because it is allied with the trawler problem, and it is one of very great importance to the fishermen in my own area. I am not going to pursue this matter further, but I would urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he takes the matter up at the United Nations to strive to achieve a little more action than we have had heretofore.

I wish to bring a matter up for a little discussion while we are still on item 1 of these estimates. I did not have the time or opportunity to do so when we were considering these estimates earlier this year. The matter about which I am concerned relates to a problem which may have been brought to the attention of a number of hon. members of the house by the united fishermen and allied workers' union of British Columbia in respect to the problem which they feel they have in connection with having representatives or observers of their organization in attendance at meetings of the various international fisheries commissions.
I realize that one might say this comes within the purview of the Department of External Affairs; nevertheless I feel it is a matter which, like a number of other matters, is of active concern to the Department of Fisheries and to members who are concerned with fisheries problems. Certainly the lead which the present Minister of Fisheries has given in the matter of international treaties I think would bear out the fact that this is a matter which can be properly raised at this time.
I think one might as well state what is part of the problem in frank terms. Part of the problem arises out of the question of the passing of communists or alleged communists across the border which exists between Canada and the United States. Part of the grievance which the fishermen's union raised was in respect to the treatment some of their members have received in an attempt to cross the border. Quite frankly I have a great deal of sympathy for them in that particular problem, because I happen to have had a little experience on one or two occasions.
I shall not elaborate on the experiences in detail, but I remember one occasion in particular when I was attempting to cross the border as a delegate to attend an international union convention and certain circumstances developed which in my opinion were rather unfortunate. The most vivid recollection I have of that incident, as a matter of fact, is that one of our delegation who happened

Supply-Fisheries
to be a member of the Liberal party of Canada was subjected to a great deal of suspicion immediately the immigration officer discovered the membership card of the Liberal party in his wallet.
As I say, that problem is one aspect of this matter, and one which I agree is not primarily the concern of the Minister of Fisheries as such. Nevertheless I think perhaps the minister would agree that attending these meetings either as an observer or an adviser by those who from time to time are chosen to represent a body such as the united fishermen and allied workers' union is a legitimate desire on their part.
Quite frankly I do not know what the solution is, in so far as we in this house can have no jurisdiction over the regulations that are put into effect from time to time by the congress of the United States, other than the solution which the fishermen's union actually did propose in one of their communications. They suggested that arrangements should be made to hold these meetings either in Canada or at some place where citizens of both countries who enjoy the normal right of freedom of movement in their respective countries would be in a position to attend if they so desired.
I have almost come to the point of suggesting to the Minister of Fisheries that he might give serious consideration to erecting a building for the holding of meetings of international bodies on the border at the Peace Arch near Blaine, one-half of which could be on one side of the border and the other half on the other side of the border. In a situation of that kind naturally the citizens of both countries would be free to be in attendance. I think this is a matter that should be receiving some consideration, in view of the number of these international commissions which we now have in which both Canada and the United States participate. I would welcome any statement on this problem which the minister might feel like making.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
As the hon. member has pointed out, this is a matter primarily for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We have Canadian members on these international commissions, and since I have been minister I have appointed one commercial fisherman on each commission so the fishermen would have a direct voice in the commissions. We have never had any trouble whatsoever with members of the commissions travelling back and forth between countries.
In addition there are advisory committees whose members are nominated by the fishermen's union, the fisheries association, the vessel owners and other groups. It is true

that on occasion certain members of these advisory committees which were picked by the fishermen's union have been stopped at the boundary on the ground that they were communists or communist sympathizers. I wrote to the union and pointed out that we have no direct control over what the United States do in the way of permitting entry into their country. I pointed out to the fishermen's union that only a fraction of one per cent of their members are communist, and therefore it should not be too hard when they know what barriers there are to choose able fishermen who are not under suspicion as being communists or communist supporters.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with what the minister has said, but I still think we should recognize that any organization should have the right to conduct its own internal affairs and select any of its people to represent it. It should be possible to make arrangements so that can be done. Whether the minister or I may consider that a man is the best delegate the union could have chosen, that in fact is not our business. Perhaps some arrangement could be made to facilitate this movement in accordance with basic democratic principles with which I think both the minister and I agree. I pointed out earlier that a member of the political organization to which the minister belongs was under definite suspicion by a certain immigration officer. This would indicate that even with the best intentions an organization such as the united fishermen and allied workers' union might have difficulty in sending perhaps the most innocent of their members across the line.

Mr. Chairman, I doubt that this has very much to do with the Minister of Fisheries, but the matter has been allowed to be brought up on the floor of the committee and I want to comment briefly upon what the Minister of Fisheries has said. He represents my views entirely. I have a large fishing population in one part of my riding, and at Steveston in my riding is located the largest cannery in the British Empire.
I am at variance with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. If I understood him rightly he said the united fishermen should be allowed to send delegates to other countries without difficulty. I want to take issue with him on that. This country has a responsibility in regard to those who are sent to other countries to represent us. As he knows and as the minister knows, if a representative of the united fishermen's union is chosen to go to another country it will be the secretary treasurer who ran against me in the last election as a labour progressive candidate. I hope the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs will never

allow that person to represent Canada in any foreign country outside of those behind the iron curtain.
I believe the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has put a slightly incorrect interpretation upon what I said.
If I did, I apologize.

I was not suggesting to the Minister of Fisheries or to the minister of external affairs that we should assume the right to choose certain citizens of our country to be sent to other countries. All I was suggesting was that the minister canvass the possibility of arranging for these commissions to meet in Canada or in line with the suggestion which I put forward, not too seriously in its exact form but nevertheless with some seriousness as far as the principle involved is concerned, to make it possible for those who might be chosen from time to time to attend as advisers or observers on behalf of the union. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has mentioned one particular member of the union and has referred to certain of his political activities. Let me make it clear at once that I am no more in agreement with the policies which that member espouses than is the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond.
I am sure of that.

Mr. Chairman, I had hoped to have spoken the first day the estimates of the Department of Fisheries were before the committee, but another hon. member was anxious to get away before we took up private and public bills that afternoon and I gave my place to him. The second day the estimates were before the committee I was on my way back from Newfoundland where I had attended a conference on northern Newfoundland affairs. I did not get back until Saturday morning, having been delayed. I had taken part in the conference during that week as it had opened on Tuesday and finished on Thursday.
I should like to draw a few points to the attention of the minister and I shall be very brief, as I did not know that these estimates were to come up this afternoon. We have heard quite a bit about the need for unemployment insurance for fishermen, and as the minister has mentioned this afternoon the fishermen are looking forward to having something done in their behalf in this regard.
There has been quite a decline in the volume of fish caught around Newfoundland during the past few years, and one reason is the lower earnings of fishermen as compared with the wages they can earn from carpentry and employment in other industries. There is 67509-309J
Supply-Fisheries
a great demand for their services at the present time. The small catch is reflected in the amount of our exports to those countries to which we have habitually been forwarding codfish. That represents less money for our people. The fact that there has been a decline is quite evident, and I think steps should be taken to counteract this decline.
The granting of 50 per cent of the cost of salt last year has been greatly appreciated by the fishermen of Newfoundland, and we are glad to hear that this is to be continued for another year. Some of us were hoping that something might be done to encourage the making of more light salted fish rather than heavy salted fish. The markets of Italy and Brazil and also Spain have a preference for that kind of fish, the slack salted, hard dried fish. This granting of the 50 per cent of the value of the salt does not really tend to improve the total catch and the total production of the light salted fish. It rather helps in the way of encouraging the heavy salted type, and much of it, of course, has been going from Newfoundland to the Nova Scotia fish plants, where they have been drying this fish which they have been buying from the Newfoundland fishermen.
Last year I spoke about the need for encouraging a better cure for fish. I understood from the minister that he would make certain studies in that regard. I should like him to let the house know what have been the results of his studies in this regard, because I think it would definitely be of great advantage to give some positive inducement to the fishermen in order that they would make more light salted fish. If some inducement in that regard were offered to the fishermen, it would be a means of encouraging them to do that.
The only other matter to which I would like to draw the minister's attention at this time is that I consider something should be done to increase the number of cullers, who have to cull the salt cod which come in from the fishermen. It is no easy matter to stand up and pass judgment on the fish, but there have to be cullers. Whilst it is not a job that many people relish, because they are often called into question, I would suggest that a school be set up or some instruction be given to the younger men in order that they might be in a position where they could more easily grade the different qualities of fish that are presented to them. If the government took a step in this direction I think it would be very helpful to the industry.

I rise at this point on a specific item which has to do, as I understand it, with the operation and maintenance of the protection branch. First of all let me say that I was very pleased to hear the minister's statement earlier, in referring to the remarks made on the first item by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, on the matter of the salary levels of some of his officials in the field, and I am glad that some adjustment has been made there. I was certainly in agreement with the remarks made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich earlier this year.
The other point I wish to raise is in connection with the field service officers of the department, and in particular with respect to the question of the patrolmen who are hired on a seasonal basis, as I understand it, every year. This question was brought to my attention during some of the travels in which I engaged during the last recess. It is in respect to what I understand to be a new regulation

calling for the compulsory retirement of patrolmen at the age of 65.
I might state briefly that it was brought to my attention in one instance by one of the patrolmen. If it had been only a matter of that single instance I might not have considered it was a matter to raise at this time, but from other conversations I have had with fishermen and people who have a knowledge of the fisheries and the functioning of the protection service on the coast, it does appear to me that this compulsory retirement in all cases of the patrolmen at the age of 65-if that is actually the situation-is something which could very well militate against the effectiveness of the protection service which is maintained on the coast of British Columbia. The minister would probably agree with me that in many cases the patrolmen who are engaged by the department are senior fishermen who have had a good many years of active experience in the game of fishing, and in some cases according to anecdotes to which I have listened-

On clause 1-Exhibitions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: May we have an explanation of this bill? It is a rather important one, and I think there is a good deal of interest in it on the part of hon. members of the house. Is the sponsor of the bill going to say anything about these various sections.

This is a bill amending the charter of the maritime stock breeders' association, which was passed by this house in 1922. I might say that the maritime stock breeders' association is the concern which sponsors the Maritime winter fair at Amherst in the constituency of my friend the hon. member for Cumberland.
The only change we are asking for is this. In the original incorporation the association was given the privilege of holding exhibitions of livestock. We are now asking, in addition to that, for the privilege of holding exhibitions of livestock, agricultural produce and any other products, goods or services produced on or for a farm, and also to make available its facilities for the purchase or sale of any such livestock or other such agricultural produce, products, goods or services.
The second clause is a new one. Formerly the association had not the power to borrow money. It is now seeking the power to borrow money in order that it may temporarily finance. Formerly the money was advanced by the directors. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 121, to amend the Canada Elections Act.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: Before the mover of the bill closes the debate, if there are no other speakers I should like to say a few words on this matter. I have forgotten the date upon which we had this bill up for second reading, but it was many weeks ago.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: It was March 9.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
At that time the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard) spoke on this matter and presented certain facts to the house which I think are relevant, because I have had the opportunity of sitting on the committee of this house which has dealt with the elections act and proposed amendments over a period of six or seven years, ever since I have been in this house.
This matter contained in the proposed bill, or at least the important phase of it which is the matter of the advance polls, has been considered by that committee on various occasions. Evidence has been taken and views have been strongly presented, but in every case of which I have knowledge the committee has decided that it was not advisable to adopt this proposal.
I think many arguments could be advanced in its favour. I believe one of the things which many people overlook is the difference between our election act and the election acts of Great Britain and other parts of the commonwealth. As I understand it, we are the only part of the commonwealth which does not have a closed election list which enables them to be ready for an election at any time. You get your certificate that you are entitled to vote; therefore elections can be brought on very
Canada Elections Act
quickly and with very few complications. In our country, for reasons which apparently are justified because of conditions which prevail here, we have never adopted that practice. Our lists are prepared at election time and that involves a great deal of time and expense. Arguments which may apply in other jurisdictions with respect to this matter, therefore, I do suggest do not apply here.
Now, of course, it is very easy to argue, and it is desirable, that everyone be given an opportunity to vote no matter what the circumstances may be; that is the idea. It is perhaps difficult to argue against that. It is always difficult to argue against something which has a theoretical appeal. We all realize that people are deprived of a vote because of the fact that occasionally they have to be away. I think it is desirable that the elections committee of this house, when that committee is set up again, should consider, as was recommended as I recall it at our last session, enlarging to some extent the scope of the advance poll so as to give more people an opportunity to vote. In fact I believe that scope has been enlarged during the time I have served on the committee.
The proposal contained in this bill is to the effect that any person who signs a declaration that he intends to or thinks he will be away on election day, can vote at the advance poll. As I recall it, the Secretary of State put certain financial considerations on the record which I think should be considered by this house, although they are not definitive and should not be taken as absolute. The mere fact that it is going to cost the country something additional should not be the yardstick we use in deciding whether or not we are going to give people the vote. Nevertheless, it is somewhat of an important factor.
I have discussed this matter with the chief electoral officer, who is an official of the house, and as I recall it he told me, although I did not take time to look up the record, that in the last election we had 243 advance polls in Canada. If this bill is adopted the chief electoral officer assumes we would have to have one advance poll for every 5 polls in urban areas and one advance poll for every 15 polls in rural areas, or approximately 5,000 more advance polls. If we take the cost as it was the last time, $130 a poll, you will see that it means a substantial increase in cost to the treasury. As I say, it is only one factor, but it is one which we have to consider.
There is also the factor that you are going to have a miniature general election over a period of three days instead of one. At the
4882	HOUSE OF
Canada Elections Act
moment everyone knows pretty well who is entitled to vote at the advance poll. The classes are defined and you make your preparations accordingly, in so far as manning the polls is concerned by the chief electoral officer, as well as by the political parties who may or may not decide to be represented at those polls. If you are going to have a situation where anyone may come in and vote it is going to result in a miniature general election for a period of three days rather than one. I assume that would mean that the political parties would have to be represented at these polls.
Again that may or may not be a matter of expense, and as I say expense should not be the definitive factor in this question. It would mean extra expense in most ridings, certainly in the urban areas, though I think there are some rural areas where workers can be found on a voluntary basis and where they would be shocked at the thought of being paid for their services. But I am told there are many areas, and I can see the practice developing even in the rural areas in the maritimes which I think is reprehensible, where you have to pay people to work for a political party at election time.
In urban areas, if you have to employ agents and scrutineers for a period of three days instead of for the one day which is generally the practice, it means that at least this is going to aggravate the problem of getting candidates, running elections, and so forth. I think also it involves the fact that candidates would have to be nominated at least one week earlier than has been the practice heretofore.
That is what the chief electoral officer advised the committee a year ago, and I think we have to take his judgment on this because he is an experienced officer, and certainly a very fair one, and one whose judgment I am sure this house will accept. He says it involves the nomination of candidates for at least three weeks prior to an election rather than the two weeks which has prevailed heretofore. That may or may not be an important factor but, generally speaking, there has been the feeling that there has been difficulty in the past when political parties nominated candidates too early. That is another reason why I think one should consider this very carefully.
I think an important factor above all which hon. members should consider, particularly those from urban areas-and certainly it does not concern me because I come from a rural area-is that in an urban area you would have a situation where a person could vote on an advanced poll certificate. All he would have to do would be to sign a declaration that he thought he was going to be 

away on election day. The opportunities for impersonation are such that what may have happened in certain urban areas in the past will, to use a slang expression, seem like a Sunday school picnic compared with what will happen if this provision comes into effect.
I have heard these arguments pro and con over the past years. I have listened to evidence of various people dealing with the suggestion. The committee representing all parties in this house gave careful consideration to those representations, and in each case the committee decided by a very substantial majority that it was not in the public interest to enlarge the advance poll to the extent that is proposed in this bill, though recognizing the theoretical advisability of giving everyone a chance to vote.
Opposed to that would be the practical and mechanical difficulties, to say nothing of the cost, which could be imposed on the other side. In every case the committee has voted against this proposal. My own feeling, Mr. Speaker, is that the committee adopted the proper procedure on those occasions. As one who has gone through it in past years, I cannot support the bill at this time.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word or two on this matter. I have had a little experience with elections, and I believe we should make it as easy as possible for people to cast their votes in our elections.
One criticism that is being made everywhere about democratic elections is that people are no longer interested in them. We cannot get the vote out. In municipal elections the number of voters is as small as 30 per cent. In my opinion we should do anything we can to make it easier for people to vote at an election without, of course, irregularities.
I am not greatly impressed with the argument of additional costs made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. I have noticed that in almost every department of life when anything new is suggested there is always opposition to it. Once it is accepted nobody would think of doing away with it. The class of people who can vote at advance polls has been changed from time to time. At one time it was reserved for railroad men and commercial travellers. As hon. members know, a person can cease to be a commercial traveller, still be a member of the commercial travellers' association and carry his card in that association, and vote at an advance poll as long as he lives.
The number of people who may be away from their homes on election day is increasing

because of changes in our way of life. A few years ago very few people in this country, with the exception of professional and wealthy people, had holidays. Now almost everybody has holidays and they get them at different times. We found that because the last election was held at the time it was, a great many people were prevented from voting because they were away on holidays. We should use every means we can, with all the safeguards that are necessary, to make it easy for people to vote. If a man or woman knows that on election day he or she is going to be away and would like to cast a vote and takes steps to do that, we should look upon it as an indication of good citizenship and we should help that person to perform his or her good citizenship function.
I imagine at all elections, if voters know the right people, they can vote at an advance poll whether they fall within the class who vote at an advance poll or not. I am going to give a little incident that I have knowledge of myself because it happened to me. I shall not mention names or dates, because in agreeing to this I may have committed an offence under the Canada Elections Act. On the Friday night preceding the election a man called me up and said, "Angus, I would like to vote for you on Monday, but I am a contractor. I have a contract in Victoria and I have to be there. Is there any way by which I can vote at an advance poll?" I said, "No, there is not. There is no way by which you can legally vote at an advance poll, but I will give you a tip. You go to the headquarters of the Liberal party and tell them of your predicament but do not tell them whom you are going to vote for. Then call me up on Saturday night before you leave for Victoria and tell me how you got along". Well, he called me up on Saturday night and said, "I voted". I knew he would vote if I sent him to the right people. I did not ask him how he voted.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: Was he not a travelling salesman instead of a contractor?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
I do not know what he was when he voted, but he was a contractor before and he was a contractor after he voted. What he was during the time he cast his vote is not material. We should use every means we can to get people to vote and to vote honestly. We should use every means we can to keep people from having to use subterfuges to perform their duties of citizenship.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre may be too wide. Perhaps it is; I do not know. If it is too wide we should accept the principle sympathetically. If we cannot accept it today we should refer it to the next meeting 67509-310
Canada Elections Act
of the elections committee, and I am quite sure that if we discuss it with the sympathy it deserves we shall increase the number of people who will be able to cast their ballots at advance polls because they will be away from their homes legitimately on election day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this bill was debated on March 9 the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard), speaking for the government, indicated his opposition to the bill, though he did profess sympathy with my contention that it should be made possible for everyone who is on the voters' list to vote.
The arguments the Secretary of State advanced against the bill were mainly two. In the first place it was his view that if it were made possible for anyone whose name is on the voters' list to vote at the advance poll there might be a tendency for great numbers of people to vote at the advance poll and leave only 60 per cent or half the population to vote on the ordinary polling day. He felt that that would be injurious to the interest in general elections, and for that reason he was not sympathetic to the bill. He also indicated there were certain technical difficulties in connection with carrying out a procedure of this kind. It was mainly on those two grounds, if I remember correctly, that he felt the government could not accept the bill.
The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska also spoke in opposition to the bill, and as I recall it he echoed the sentiments expressed by the Secretary of State. He also expressed some surprise and perhaps concern over the fact that if this bill went through people simply going off on trips to Winnipeg would be able to vote before they left on such a desirable journey.
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that I think the Secretary of State put up a rather absurd argument when he suggested that a large percentage of people would vote at the advance poll even though they were not going to be away from home on election day. The reason I think that argument is absurd is that we already have universal voting at advance polls in a number of the provinces in this country. It happens in my home city of Winnipeg in the province of Manitoba in provincial elections, and although more people percentage-wise take advantage of that right than is the case in federal elections-because of the difference in the law-still the number is not great at all.

Canada Elections Act

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: That does not make the argument absurd, I believe; but it might well be that the situation would become such in a dominion general election.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: I think it is pretty difficult for the Secretary of State to argue from no known facts to the position he takes. I think it is much more logical to deduce what would happen from a parallel situation that already exists.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: But it does increase, does it not?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
No, and there are other hon. members from other provinces, as a matter of fact, who have expressed the same surprise at that argument. I do not think there is any question but that the general interest would be in the ordinary day of polling, the general election day. All we are asking for here is that those who find they have to be away from home for any reason be given the right to vote at an advance poll.
As to the technical difficulties in carrying out a matter of this kind, I recognize them readily. I did so, as a matter of fact, when I spoke in introducing the bill on second reading. I was able to indicate on that occasion, and express my appreciation in doing so, that I had assistance from two of our officials, the chief electoral officer and our parliamentary counsel, in the preparing of the bill. I take the responsibility for what is in the bill, but I did have their advice and assistance in putting it together, and I suggest that it does contain practical ways in which this principle of the right of anyone who has to be away to vote at the advance poll can be preserved.
Nevertheless, as I suggested when I moved second reading of the bill on March 9, these technical difficulties constitute the kind of details that can be discussed if this bill can have second reading and then be referred to a committee. In other words, Mr. Speaker, what we are dealing with at this point is the principle rather than the details of the bill, and the principle is very simple and clear; namely, that if we are going to have advance polls the right to vote at an advance poll should not be restricted to a limited category of people but should be extended to all who find they will be away from their homes on election day.
As to the point raised by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska regarding people who go on trips, let there be no doubt about it, Mr. Speaker; one of the main reasons I have presented this bill and one of the main reasons it has support from certain sections of the community to which I shall refer in a moment, is because it is now true that more people have holidays than used to be the case.


It is also true that elections generally seem to come in the summer period. In recent years elections have been held in June or in August or in October, if we go back to 1935. I think it is generally recognized that barring some unexpected event that would force an election at an unexpected time, elections will continue to be held in the summer period. Let there be no secret about it; this bill is advanced partly in order that people who rightly go away on holidays might have the right to vote. Surely going away on a holiday is not a crime for which one should lose his right as a citizen to vote at a general election.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: Legitimate business.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Some people who go away can get back from their holidays, depending on how far away they are or how much money they have to spend to make the trip back home, but for a great many people that is impossible. We feel the citizens of the country should be entitled to vote even if a general election comes in the period they are away on holidays, and that is precisely one of the reasons for presenting this bill.
I shall not take further time to repeat the arguments I made in presenting the bill on March 9, for the obvious reason is that if a vote has to be taken I would not want to keep the house here past six o'clock, so I shall conclude with just this further comment.
Hon. members will recall that they have received, if their experience is similar to mine, quite a few letters in support of Bill No. 121 which is now before them, and I think they will recognize that these letters in the main have come from two types of organizations. They have come on the one hand from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and from local chambers of commerce. They have come on the other hand from labour organizations. I think that makes it pretty clear this is the kind of bill that appeals to a cross section of the community, for surely if you take those who are represented by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and those who are represented by the labour organizations of this country you have a very large section of the Canadian population. As hon. members are aware, these organizations have given their support to the principle of this bill and have urged that this house give it a favourable vote at this time.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, if the house agrees to the second reading of this bill it would then be my suggestion that it be referred for further study to the committee on privileges and elections.
My friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has expressed surprise at my suggesting that it be referred to the committee on

privileges and elections. The reason for that, if I may say so to my colleague, is that the last time the Canada Elections Act was under consideration by a committee of the house, instead of a special committee being set up it was referred to the committee on privileges and elections.

I suppose it would be possible for the entire population to vote at the advance polls instead of on the general polling day, but if I may say so without offending my hon. friend, for I do not want to do that, 67509-3104
Canada Elections Act
I think the suggestion that that would happen is in the realm of absurdity. I do not think it would happen in a federal general election any more than it has happened in provincial general elections in my own province of Manitoba. I think the interest of our people would still be in the general election day, but at the same time this measure would remove one of the most serious grievances we come up against in every general election, when people come into the committee rooms of the various parties and into the headquarters of the returning officer wondering why it is that although there are advance polls no vote is available to them. The purpose of this bill is to correct that situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: On Monday we shall take interim supply and, if that is passed, we shall take the resolution with respect to the Canadian National Railway Company financing, the resolution in the name of the Minister of National Defence with respect to the Defence Services Pension Act, etc., and second reading of the bill in my name in respect to the Tariff Board Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: Could I ask the Prime Minister if he has yet reached a decision as to whether there will be an adjournment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, it has not been possible to reach any decision since this morning.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: I would point out simply, so the position may be clear, that to ask for one month's interim supply with the possibility of adjournment creates a situation which cannot be disregarded. We are not dealing with a normal situation, if there is one month's supply and then an adjournment for several months, and for that reason I think that in asking for any consideration of the procedure that should be adopted it is essential that we know exactly what the position will be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: We could not suggest an adjournment after having obtained only one month's supply.
